PETITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour, on behalf of a number of people in western Canada, to present a petition on the subject of the trade deal the Government negotiated with the United States.
These people are very concerned about the future of Canadian sovereignty, and believe it has been compromised through this agreement. They are afraid that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has threatened the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty by removing the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership, to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interests of Canadians, and to equalize opportunities between the regions. They also believe that the agreement would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future, and undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States.
For those and other reasons the petitioners humbly call upon Parliament to dissolve and let the people of Canada have the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade arrangement through a national general election.

The House resumed from Monday, February 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this House agrees with amendments 8 and 13(e) made by the Senate to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, but disagrees with amendments 4, 5(a), (b) and (c), 6(a) and (b), 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13(a) because this House believes they contradict the principles of the Bill for the following reasons:
Amendment 4 would exclude only criminals and war criminals from the refugee determination process, but would allow terrorists, spies and subversives to pursue a claim to refugee status, notwithstanding the fact that Article 33 of the UN Convention would permit the removal of these latter individuals to their countries of nationality or permanent residence, even if they were determined to be Convention refugees.
Amendment 5(a) would eliminate the authority of the Minister to direct a ship to leave or not to enter Canadian waters. This amendment would reopen a significant gap in Canada's ability to control its borders.
Amendments 5(b) and (c) arise out of Senate amendment 5(a), which is not acceptable, and are therefore inappropriate.
Amendments 6(a) and (b) would reverse the policy on which the Immigration Act, 1976 was based, which policy was not changed in the Bill as passed by this House. The amendments jeopardize the possibility of successfully prosecuting persons who profit from organizing illegal migration and from counselling fraud among refugee claimants.
Amendments 9 and 10 would restrict the ability of peace officers and immigration officers to act quickly to search for evidence of major offences under the Immigration Act, 1976, in exigent circumstances, where lives are at risk or where evidence with respect to those offences may be lost or destroyed.
Amendments 11 and 12 would restrict the ability of peace officers and immigration officers to execute search warrants which have been duly authorized by a justice of the peace, by denying explicit authority to break open containers where it is reasonably believed evidence will be found and by limiting the authority to execute these warrants at night.
Amendment 13(a) would reduce the initial period of detention without review from seven days to forty-eight hours, which would allow insufficient time for the gathering of information to substantiate allegations or to identify

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate being recognized this morning to make some comments on Bill C-84. We have had a good debate on this Bill. We are discussing, of course, the Government's motion in response to the Senate's reaction to this Bill. My hon. friend

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
from Spadina very eloquently presented my Party's position on this government initiative. I thought he had done the job so well, as had a number of my colleagues, that this round of debate would be ended after another two or three interjections. However, a number of things encouraged me to change my mind earlier this morning and I have decided to say a few words.
Earlier today I was handed a telegram from the Council of Christian Reform Churches. It brought to my attention that the government motion on Bill C-84 is very inadequate and unacceptable. They believe it is unacceptable in the way it relates to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in how it refers to the United Nations Convention for Refugees, about which 1 will have more to say in a moment. When the Christian Reform Churches brought to my attention that there were some real problems with this government initiative I decided to explore it a bit further.
This morning I was also handed a lengthy telegram from the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees. The Inter-Church Committee for Refugees said that the government response to the Senate refugee Bill report is unacceptable. They said:
The Senate undertook a serious study of Bill C-84 and made minimal changes to make it constitutional and thus workable. There was no room for compromise.
The government response denies persons their right to have a refugee claim heard by insisting on calling them a security risk or turning away boats. That is an unacceptable and unnecessary denial of individual rights.
That phrase, "turning away boats", reminded me of an incident which happened many years ago in our country. I received a number of phone calls over the weekend from constituents of mine who are of the Sikh religion, They reminded me of the Kamagata Maru incident which occurred on our West Coast.
At that time a number of people from India wished to come to Canada to make Canada their home. They chartered a boat, certainly not a liner or a passenger ship, but a regular freighter which was their home for many weeks as they journeyed from Bombay and other parts of India, primarily the Punjab region. They arrived on the coast of British Columbia in the Port of Vancouver and wanted to make Canada their home.
The Canadian officials with the Port Authority in Vancouver, and I regret to say with the support of the federal Government of the day, held that boat in the port day after day as the Government of the day tried to find ways of stopping these people from landing and becoming Canadian citizens. One of the saddest days in our history was when the federal Government decided to use our naval gunboats to force that ship to return to a port in India. Those Sikh immigrants were forced to return to their homeland against their wishes and their will.
The Kamagata Maru incident, as it is now referred to, is a very dark mark on our history. There are others. As an example, a ship carrying Jewish refugees fleeing persecution in Nazi Germany and other parts of Europe came to Canada and
the Canadian Government forced it to return to Europe. We did not want to welcome those refugees at the time. The federal government of the day thought this was inappropriate and forced the boat to return to Europe. I am afraid to say that sources tell us that virtually all of those people eventually met death at the hands of the Nazi war machine.
[DOT] (U20)
Most of us are well aware of those two incidents. We now find that this legislation includes a clause that would give the federal authorities the right to intercept a ship coming into Canadian waters with alleged illegal refugees onboard and the right to force that ship to turn about and return to its port of origin or some other port. In other words, someone would determine that the people onboard were illegal refugees, but 1 do not know how that could be determined by flying over the ship or quickly visiting it without allowing due process to hear those people claiming to be refugees. Quite frankly, it makes me shiver because it conjures up images of the Kamagata Maru incident or the incident when we forced the ship with people of Jewish faith to return to Europe.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees has repeatedly made it clear that a denial of access actually violates the intent of the U.N. Convention on Refugees. As a matter of fact, a United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees spokesperson who testified before the legislative committee examining Bill C-84 said that, "According to the provisions of the convention, it is necessary to determine if the person is a refugee or not." He went on to say, "During the refugee determination procedure it is always possible to discover whether the person committed a serious crime of a non-political nature, but it is necessary first to proceed to a determination of refugee status."
There are many concerns about this legislation, but 1 am reminded by my constituents of the Kamagata Maru incident. The Government still insists on maintaining a clause in Bill C-84 by which the Kamagata Maru incident could occur again. That is something of which I and my Party want no part, and we identify this as a dark day in Canadian history. We describe this as a very racist act of a past government and something that ought to have no place in Canada in the past, present or future.
I cannot imagine that anyone in the House would want to accept the fact that this Bill enshrines this kind of behaviour as part of Government legislation. Personally, I welcome the amendments that were adopted unanimously in the Senate. While I do not agree with that particular institution, their amendments to Bill C-84 are good. They follow very closely the amendments which my Party moved when this matter was debated in the House. They would correct the main flaws of this Bill and, therefore, 1 regret that the Government has rejected the majority of the Senate amendments, including amendments which the Government accepted in principle but then whittled away most of their meaning.
February 2, 1988

I regret that the Government has chosen to rush this Bill in after months of delay, with so little time for Members to read it before debate is completed. I want to congratulate Members of the New Democratic Party and those in the Liberal Party who have spoken out about the major shortcomings that still exist in Bill C-84. The Government has failed to listen to virtually every individual and group with experience in the area of refugees. I believe there were dozens and dozens of qualified groups with great experience in matters dealing with immigration and refugees that universally condemned this Bill. All pointed out major shortcomings in Bill C-84, yet their voice was ignored by the Government. I find that rather arrogant and 1 question whether the Government is serious in its intention to bring forth legislation that is consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and with the United Nations Charter dealing with refugees. This Bill fails on these two counts. On that note I will conclude my remarks to allow others an opportunity to raise their concerns.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's comments are ones that we have heard many times before, not only from the Hon. Member but other Members of his Party and the Liberal Opposition. The remarks really repeat what has been said during a very lengthy debate on Bill C-84, when it was first before the House for debate on second reading, then at third reading, report stage and at committee stage.
We are now into what I believe can be reasonably described as the longest filibuster of any matter coming back from the Senate that has occurred during the course of this Parliament. The Hon. Member indicated that he was in support of all the amendments that came from the Senate.
The Government has specifically rejected amendment No. 4. In fact, the Liberal Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) has moved an amendment to these proceedings which would put the Senate amendment No. 4 into place. The effect of that, of course, would be that refugee claimants who are criminals, and war criminals, would be excluded from the refugee determination process but the terrorists, spies and subversives would be allowed to continue through the process.
It is my understanding that Article 33 of the U.N. Convention provides that where there are reasonable grounds for regarding a refugee claimant as a danger to the security of the country in which he or she is, that article would permit the removal of the individual from Canada even if it were determined that such person was a convention refugee. Does the Hon. Member agree with the amendment put forward by the Liberal Member for York West that would allow terrorists, spies and subversives to make a claim for refugee status in this country?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on the refugee question and on Bill C-84. I am particularly concerned about this issue. While there was a real problem which needed addressing, the Government has handled it in the wrong way. I believe that a large part of the responsibility for the problems we face with the backlog of refugees seeking determination under the present process must fall upon the present Government.
1 do not want to deal with this at length, but I would remind Hon. Members that it has now been some two and half to three years since we received the report of Rabbi Plaut on refugees and it has been something over two years since we received the report of the employment and immigration committee. That report represented a consensus on a workable means for putting into place a more effective refugee determination process.
If the Government had been prepared to listen to the recommendations that had been made at that time and if it had been prepared to go along with them, we would now have an effective determination system working. After a couple of years, if contentions made by refugee-aid groups, by opposition
Parties, by the churches, by Amnesty International and by a whole range of people involved in the refugee question were that the procedure did not prove to be workable, perhaps some further amendments to the process might then have been needed. Instead of that, the Government continues to reject the bulk of the amendments which came back from the Senate.
I am normally not an advocate of the Senate of Canada. 1 believe it is an outdated body and 1 do not think that having an appointed body as one of the Chambers of this Parliament makes a great deal of sense. I believe that the Senate should be abolished. However, it exists now. It has a Constitutional role and, for once, it is trying to redeem a pretty tawdry record by doing its constitutional job of being a Chamber of sober second thought.
I find it interesting that a Chamber of this House, which has traditionally been known as a defender of the privileged and wealthy and as a body which ignores the needs of average Canadians, should have been so convinced by the evidence presented to its committee which laboured long and hard on Bill C-84 that it came back to the House with 13 amendments. These amendments would turn this Bill which is unworkable, unfair, unconstitutional and would sully Canada's international reputation, into a piece of legislation which my Party and most people concerned with refugees would be able to support. It does not make it perfect.
We recognize that some difficult compromises may need to be made, but there is the wherewithal for reasonable compromise in this particular area in the amendments put forward by the Senate. However, rather than going along with that and rather than trying to build a certain amount of consensus and support from the people concerned with the refugee process, the Government continues to bull ahead, accepting only two or three of the recommendations from the Senate. It then put forward a motion which essentially would reject most of those amendments.
If the Government still believes that the Senate should exist, then it should be prepared to accept that the Senate does function and that its constitutional mandate is to function as a chamber of sober second thought. We are not talking here about the Senate trying to undo a major tax Bill, or about the Senate trying to reverse economic policy being made by the Government of Canada. Those functions properly belong in the House of Commons. We are talking about sober second thought after detailed consideration of a difficult topic.
Under those circumstances I have to say that until we get rid of the Senate or until the Government says that it does not acknowledge any validity in terms of the Senate's operations and it will get rid of it as soon as it can, then the Government should be prepared to listen to the suggestions that the Senate has made and to give them positive consideration. It does not necessarily mean that the Government should adopt all 13 recommendations. It does mean that it should be prepared to
February 2, 1988

give enough consideration so that the bulk of the 13 representations will be accepted. Of course, that has not occurred. The consequence is that we are back to where we began in this affair. We are back to a situation in which we have an unacceptable response from the Government.

The refugee issue will remain a controversial one and will continue to generate appeals to our courts of law, all the way up to the Supreme Court. Last week after the decision on the Morgentaler case, we saw how the Supreme Court was prepared to apply the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to every jurisdiction of the Government of Canada. If before last Thursday, the Government was unwilling to respond to the constitutional concerns of the Senate with respect to Bill C-84, it should be willing to do so now.
Mr. Speaker, 1 am personally very disturbed about two questions. First, the matter of precluding from the refugee system people found to be security risks, without further specification, instead of specifying only those refugees who are indeed a threat to Canada's security. There was a brief period of parliamentary democracy in Zaire, but now they have a situation where it seems General Mobutu, the country's dictator, has actually extracted a fortune of $5 billion from his people and put it in Swiss banks.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak on this Bill; I have not spoken on it before. I feel that it is an extremely important Bill. Certainly in my riding of Yukon we have a number of refugees who have made a significant contribution to the community and to the territory as a whole. They are certainly well respected by the other people in the community and territory.
It was interesting for me during the break to have the opportunity to travel to a number of communities in my riding and to speak with students in January when the schools were reopened. This issue was raised by many students. They were very confused about what were immigrants and what were refugees. I guess they reflected the gambit of opinion which one often sees throughout Canada.
I am pleased to speak to the matter today because it is an area which is still somewhat confusing to many people in Canada. I am also pleased to support many of the Senate amendments. Like many of my colleagues, I do so with some difficulty since I have some problem with the authority of that body. However, in this particular case the Senate has listened to the comments from across Canada. It has heard many of the same people who were heard by the legislative committee, and it has responded in a very reasoned way by proposing a number of quite useful amendments.
The issue is not really one of taking too much time for debate; it is an extremely serious issue in Canada. We see that in the general public on the one hand there are remarks which seem to reflect an attitude that somehow Canada is being taken advantage of, that somehow someone is doing something to us over which we do not have control, and that we must have better control. I think other groups of people who have worked with refugees, have assisted refugees, and have travelled abroad, more clearly understand the very pathos and tragedy of people who become refugees. We see a debate which sometimes does not just dwell on the facts of the case but on the impressions of people.
The impression of one group that the refugees about whom we are talking are somehow taking advantage of us in Canada
and are misrepresenting themselves is perhaps true in some cases. Certainly it does not describe, by far, the majority of refugees. Therefore, my Party and I say that there must be some improved ways to ensure that people who come to Canada presenting themselves as refugees are truly in need of protection.
On the other hand Canada cannot abrogate its role and its well deserved reputation for responding in a humanitarian way to the needs of those who are in situations in their own countries which put their lives, their families, and their wellbeing in jeopardy.
A further point which the Senate amendments have addressed is that of the constitutionality of Bill C-84. When we hear Members speak of the high cost of this debate, taking up taxpayers' funds, we have to see if we can bring some reason into this debate for the Government to support some of the reasoned amendments which will save taxpayers' money, otherwise there will be many charter challenges and a lot of money will be spent in the courts.
1 would like to return to the issue that I addressed early. There is great confusion between what is an immigrant and what is a refugee, and why a refugee and an immigrant come to this country. Many witnesses at committee hearings and many commentators have pointed out that because of the many problems in our immigration system this has led to a backlog of people awaiting entry to Canada. Our inability to deal with that backlog has exacerbated the problem of access to this country by legitimate refugees. People who, in other circumstances, would be immigrants as opposed to refugees, are representing themselves as refugees. This is a serious problem that needs to be addressed. The Government felt it was so serious that it recalled Parliament on an emergency basis to deal with it.
The issue is fundamental; the two systems are not working well together, namely, our immigration system and the rules relating to refugees. I want to say a few words about what it means to be a refugee. For those of us who have been fortunate to have lived in Canada all our lives and have not been faced with threats to our lives or well-being because of our views, it is often very difficult to imagine what it would be like if that were not the case. That is why we have so much public debate on the issue. Most of us who have lived in security find this difficult to understand.

Mr. Speaker, I quite understand what the Bill is about and we are trying to deal with those people who are misrepresenting themselves as refugees. I am attempting to say, perhaps not articulately enough for the Member across the floor, that often there is a misunderstanding about what a refugee is and what a refugee can do. I think this Bill reflects some of that misunderstanding.
For example, to suggest that a refugee can go to a country's local immigration office, receive all the proper documentation then leave that country with the blessing of the officials and blithely come here to present the proper documentation, is incorrect. If that were the case, we would not be discussing the question of fraud and misrepresentation. Refugees do not have that option. They are often in a situation, as the Member well knows, where their lives are in danger if they speak out and they cannot go to the local office, get all the proper documentation and blithely leave their country. If we limit access to those seeking asylum to those travelling by airlines, legislating that the airlines must require and control documentation; if we insist on proper forms of visas and transit visas, and forcibly return people from border points, the only right that people would have would be to stay in their countries, be tortured, detained or killed. That is what we are talking about.
To counteract that, we are suggesting that every person who comes here has the right to be heard as to the legitimacy of whether or not that individual is a refugee. We are not suggesting that every person who says he or she is a refugee should automatically be accepted on that word. But we have to accept the reality that a person may not be able to get the kind of documentation this Bill suggests should be obtained. That is not an appropriate or realistic, but rather a punitive and unrealistic form of control.
What is being suggested by the amendments and by my Party is that we should have a process in place where a person can state his or her case in a full hearing about whether or not that person is a refugee. It is at that point that those who may misrepresent themselves will be identified and not accepted as refugees.
I want to say again that we cannot categorize all people as misrepresenting themselves in order to ensure that the few people who do will not be accepted. There is a compromise position presented in these amendments. It is a position which I believe, and which many others believe, will address the problem and ensure that we carry out our humanitarian obligations, not contravening the very constitutional base of this country. We must also make sure that we do not allow in people who are not genuine refugees, who can apply through the other immigration process.
I feel very strongly that we must as a country keep our deserved humanitarian reputation, while at the same time we

must have appropriate systems and mechanisms in place to ensure fairness for immigrants and refugees. I believe these amendments would go a long way toward addressing that.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
REGIONAL ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. Quebecers, Montrealers are really disappointed in the Prime Minister of Canada. They expected him to unveil programs to promote the economic renewal of Montreal East. We expected him to announce, when he was in Montreal, that in co-operation with the provincial Government he would inject $25 million to establish a business modernization and restructuring office, that he would commit considerable amounts of money toward training programs, the employability of Montreal East workers and the eligibility under the Program for Older Worker Adjustment.
We also expected the Prime Minister of Canada to select Montreal as the site of the Space Agency, to offer a $130 million expansion of the old harbour and money for the development of the Montreal harbour, but the people of Quebec also expected the Prime Minister to announce redress for the Lauzon, Sorel and Montreal shipyards that have been unjustly treated.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, all the Prime Minister did when he came to Montreal, to City Hall and the Chamber of commerce was clown about. Nothing concrete was announced for the people of Montreal and Quebec.

subtopic: BILL C-84-TIME SPENT ON DEBATE
BILL C-84-TIME SPENT ON DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an historical day in the House of Commons. We are now in the sixth day of a Liberal/NDP coalition filibuster on Bill C-84, a Bill which is extremely important to Canada's future. This Bill is aimed at preventing the abuse of Canada's generosity and humanitarianism by getting control of our borders. The measures in this Bill are aimed at those who jeopardize the safety of legitimate refugees and imperil the security of Canadian citizens.
This filibuster is costing Canadians almost half a million dollars per day. Is this the style of low-handed dealings that Canadians could expect if we were ever unfortunate enough to experience a coalition of those two Parties? Rather than continuing to stall a Bill which is supported by the majority of Canadians, those two Parties should let Parliament get on with the business of passing Bills for the betterment of our citizens.

February 2, 1988
It is time that we asked the Canadian people if they want an opportunistic coalition or a common-sense Government. Let's call an election!

subtopic: CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES
CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 do not know if the United Nations has proclaimed 1988 the year of CBC bashing, but this Conservative Government certainly has. The onslaught began last week when the Communications Minister succumbed to the petty and vindictive whinings of many of her caucus colleagues and put on hold indefinitely a CBC all-news channel. Conservatives believe that if you control the messenger you can control the message. The Minister's decision was a blatant, thinly veiled effort to muzzle the CBC.
Today we learn of yet another attack on the corporation. Now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Secretary of State are getting into the act. They are working with real estate friends in Toronto to scuttle plans for a much needed national broadcast centre. Public broadcasting is under attack, and this foolhardy Conservative Government is leading the charge. It must be stopped. Let's have an election!

subtopic: BILL C-84-TIME SPENT ON DEBATE
BILL C-84-TIME SPENT ON DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Government was elected with a large majority by the people of Canada to govern the country, and the Opposition and the Senate are thwarting the will of the people.
For weeks the Liberals and the NDP coalition, along with their friends in the Senate, have stalled the passing of immigration laws desired by the majority of Canadians. These bleeding hearts want every boatload of illegal so-called refugees, and every person who tears up their papers arriving at our airports, accorded the same treatment set out for true refugees, even if they are deemed to be terrorists and security risks. "Don't turn the boats back, let them land", the Senate and the Liberal-socialist coalition cry.
For several weeks the stalling of legislation has been going on and already it has cost the Canadian people more than $3 million. The Senate and the Liberals and the NDP talk democracy but act like totalitarians. Let's call an election and get rid of these obstructionists, these bleeding hearts!

subtopic: LAVAL POSTAL EMPLOYEES-FUTURE OUTLOOK-NEED FOR GOVERNMENT TO FURNISH INFORMATION
LAVAL POSTAL EMPLOYEES-FUTURE OUTLOOK-NEED FOR GOVERNMENT TO FURNISH INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday the Minister responsible for Canada Post answered a question from my colleague from Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) concerning the closure of Laval's postal processing plant saying, I quote:

"I understand that Canada Post did brief Members of Parliament from that area with respect to its plans".

As briefings go, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that 1 first heard about the closure of Laval's postal processing plant in a telephone call from the mayor of Laval who wanted to know if I was aware of it. I also learned that the local Conservative Members had not been consulted either. Later my office got a phone call from Canada Post officials promising that I would be sent information and releases. Mr. Speaker, these documents reached me only late yesterday afternoon.
I want to take exception to the attitude of the Mulroney Government and the Minister responsible, disrespectful as they are of our representative duties as Members of the House. Laval happens to be the second largest city in Quebec. Astonishing though it may be, the Conservatives consider this city as a negligible factor, a city with over 300,000 residents which apparently does not even deserve to have a postal processing plant.
We have been told that the employees will be transferred to the Montreal downtown plant. But what will happen after that? Will they be included in the lay-offs announced in the rationalization plan to which my colleague from Saint-Leonard-Anjou referred last Friday in this House?
Mr. Speaker, the Laval postal employees have the right to know.

subtopic: NEED FOR MINISTERIAL POWER TO EXPEL SHIPS
NEED FOR MINISTERIAL POWER TO EXPEL SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Senate is seeking to deprive the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) of his authority to turn around ships which have been chartered by racketeers to bring people to Canada.
It has been argued that the best deterrent would be to bring the ships into port and confiscate them. The Minister does not share this view. He feels that it would be only a hay rake
February 2, 1988

attempt which would allow many more groups of people to enter Canada illegally.
By maintaining his power to turn ships around, even if he exercised this power on rare occasions, we would take away from the racketeers who organize illegal trips their main argument of a guaranteed access to Canada.
If the people concerned start having serious misgivings about the success of the various schemes, they might be less tempted to pay the high prices demanded by the racketeers, and the attractiveness of these organized trips would no longer be so great.
Mr. Speaker, all Hon. Members of this House will have to unite to support the amendment moved by the Minister of Employment and Immigration to turn the ships around and stop these racketeers who are organizing illegal trips to Canada.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF PORCUPINE CARIBOU HERD TO ABORIGINAL PEOPLE
IMPORTANCE OF PORCUPINE CARIBOU HERD TO ABORIGINAL PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to speak today on the release of a publication entitled "The Caribou are our Life", which outlines the importance of the Porcupine caribou herd, one of America's most unique natural resources and essential to the subsistence activities of the aboriginal people of Alaska, the Yukon, and Northwest Territories.
Today this booklet is being distributed to all Members of Parliament. I am happy to say that the Department of External Affairs has shared in the costs and supported the voices of the Yukon and Northwest Territories in speaking out against the opening of caribou calving grounds to oil and gas development.
What this means is that the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska must be protected from oil and gas development. We were alarmed when the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources appeared to support development in this area, a stance not previously taken by the Government.
However, clearly we now stand together in attempting to persuade the United States Government of the importance of the wise use of this land. Northerners are not opposed to development, but we know that we must respect our wilderness heritage and the aboriginal people who depend on it.
I call upon all Members of the House to support the pressure for the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.

subtopic: BILL C-84-TIME SPENT ON DEBATE
BILL C-84-TIME SPENT ON DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this minute has six days. Canadians have witnessed, for the first time in history, six days of phoney debate on Senate amendments to Bill C-84. The Conservative Government of Canada, by this Bill, will put an end to illegal and undesirable aliens from entering Canada.
Six days of stalling this Bill by a nonsensical filibuster could presently allow legal entry of terrorists into Canada. If another "Munich" occurs in Calgary or Toronto, it could very easily be blamed on the Opposition's irresponsible tactics in the House.
Higher drug prices would easily have been avoided by the new drug price review board, had the Opposition not used the same tactics when stalling Bill C-22.
If the Opposition plans to continue this filibuster in the House in such an irresponsible manner, perhaps it is time to call an election so that voters can throw them out and put mature people in their place.

subtopic: AWARD OF FRIGATE CONSTRUCTION CONTRACT TO NEW BRUNSWICK SHIPYARD-POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
AWARD OF FRIGATE CONSTRUCTION CONTRACT TO NEW BRUNSWICK SHIPYARD-POSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the NDP is having a great deal of difficulty deciding whether or not to support the awarding of the second batch of frigates to Saint John Shipbuilding Limited.
First it was the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Centre (Mr. Cassidy) stating in Quebec that his Party would reopen the contract and give Quebec half the frigates. Then the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) stated in the House that such decisions should be made after an open and honest tendering system regardless of where you live, for which I applauded him. That position was backed by his Leader who, later in the day, indicated that his Party would not re-open the contract. However, last Thursday, the NDP Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) was saying in the House:
-I want to express my astonishment at the Government's decision-to award the second half dozen frigates entirely to the Saint John shipyards-
It is particularly repugnant to Quebecers to see one particular enterprise, the Irving interests in Saint John receiving this very large contract to the detriment of the provincially owned Marine Industries-
It is time the New Democratic Party got its act together on this issue. The NDP is pitting region against region, similar to the way the Tories did with regard to the CF-18 decision. This attempt to sway the voters of the Province of Quebec is unacceptable. Such behaviour is not in the national interest.

February 2, 1988

subtopic: BOGUS REFUGEES-POSITION OF ALLEGED LIBERAL-SOCIALIST COALITION

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: BOGUS REFUGEES-POSITION OF ALLEGED LIBERAL-SOCIALIST COALITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House has been faced for the past six days with a fillibuster from the Liberal-Socialist coalition which opposes our bill aimed at stopping illegal refugees.
Does the Liberal-Socialist coalition want Canada to continue to be considered as a privileged target country by all those involved in the illegal refugee trade throughout the world?
Does the Liberal-Socialist coalition continue to support these international smugglers?
Last week, the Socialist leader wanted the Government to crucify Terrorist Mahmoud Mohammad and send him away immediately; yet, together with his party, he still refuses to adopt the necessary legislation to settle quickly the case of this terrorist.
The Liberal-Socialist coalition should make up its mind quickly, unless it wants to receive a clear message from Canadians during a general election, Mr. Speaker!

maintopic: NECESSITY FOR GOVERNMENT TO GIVE INFORMATION ON SUBJECT OF THERAPEUTIC ABORTIONS
NECESSITY FOR GOVERNMENT TO GIVE INFORMATION ON SUBJECT OF THERAPEUTIC ABORTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian women are confused since last Thursday about the procedures to be followed to obtain a therapeutic abortion. Unfortunately, they cannot turn to the federal Government for guidance, because it has not yet responded to the decision delivered by the Supreme Court. On the other hand, the provinces interpret that decision quite differently.
It is essential, Mr. Speaker, that the Tory Government clearly indicate to Canadian women, physicians and provincial governments that Section 251 of the Criminal Code can no longer set the procedure through which therapeutic abortion services are made available.
After having done that, the Government could perhaps take up the real challenge underlying the entire matter. A broad range of health services should be made available to Canadian women. For that purpose, the federal Government should finance the search for safe and effective contraceptive methods as well as the educational programs of responsible organizations such as the Planned parenthood Federation.

subtopic: BILL C-84-TIME SPENT ON DEBATE
BILL C-84-TIME SPENT ON DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have witnessed a record six-day filibuster in this House by the Liberal-Socialist coalition supporting the Liberal dominated Senate amendments to Bill C-84.
The Minister, in a spirit of co-operation and openness, has accepted several of the 18 Senate amendments. This uneces-sary filibuster has cost Canadians $3 million to date, all for the political advantage of the Socialist-Liberal coalition.
Let us stop this silliness and political grandstanding and let the democratically elected voice of Parliament get on with its job. Once again we are seeing the unelected Senate thwarting the will of the duly elected Members of Parliament from passing a progressive piece of legislation, very much needed for the protection of Canadians, and giving a fair process for all who would seek refuge in Canada.

subtopic: ETHIOPIA-FOOD SHORTAGES-PLEA FOR CANADIAN DONATIONS
ETHIOPIA-FOOD SHORTAGES-PLEA FOR CANADIAN DONATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an emergency in Ethiopia. Last November the Government of Ethiopia issued an urgent international appeal for 1.05 million tonnes of food. This appeal was subsequently increased to 1.3 million tonnes, virtually the same amount as during the 1984-85 famine which claimed the lives of approximately one million people.
Very few of us will forget the tragic scenes of starvation and death three years ago. Today, Ethiopia faces an equally urgent situation. Drought and locusts are now threatening the meagre existence of seven million Ethiopians. If we act quickly and decisively, lives can be saved. Government aid is significant but more can be done. Canadian farmers have been exceptionally generous but various fund-raising appeals to average Canadians have reported a poor response.
Do we as Canadians have to see the bloated bellies of children before we are jarred out of our complacency? I call upon our Government to provide more assistance, and at the same time urge all Canadians to help avert this famine by sending their donations to Oxfam Canada, the Canadian Red Cross, or Canadian Physicians for Aid and Relief.
February 2, 1988

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is concerned, the Prime Minister maintains that he did not discuss Mr. Gorman's letter nor the matter generally with the Minister.
Yet, Mr. Gorman's letter states that the Minister has taken part in an offence under Section 62.6 of the Canada Elections Act.
How can the Prime Minister still maintain that he does not have the duty to ask the Minister whether the facts mentioned in the letter are true or not, especially as these facts affect the credibility of his Minister as a politician and a member of his Government?

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already replied to this question. The Leader of the Official Opposition refers to a private letter apparently sent by the Commissioner to the Hon. Member for Frontenac. As for me, I referred to a public statement made on November 28, 1985, in which the Federal Elections Commissioner, Mr. Joseph Gorman, said, and I quote: "And I have decided that no charge would be laid against the Hon. Marcel Masse." Following this decision of the investigating Commissioner, 1 decided to have the Minister rejoin Cabinet.
There has already been some reference to the letter which the Leader of the Official Opposition himself described as ambiguous or remarkable. It is certainly unusual.
As for the official statement dealing with the findings of the investigating Commissioner, it was made public and I quoted it myself and acted accordingly.

subtopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister describes Mr. Gorman's letter as a private letter addressed to a Minister. Such a letter is never private and it concerns the public duties of the Minister.

subtopic: KNOWLEDGE OF CONTENTS OF LETTER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: KNOWLEDGE OF CONTENTS OF LETTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources resigned in 1985 he did so because there was suspicion that he might have violated the Canada Elections Act. At that time there were mixed signals about who knew what and when they knew it. As the Prime Minister himself has suggested, the Minister remains under suspicion as a result of Mr. Gorman's letter. The Prime Minister stated he did not know of the existence of this letter until he saw it in the press.
Oral Questions
Can the Prime Minister assure this House that neither the Secretary to the Cabinet, Mr. Tellier, nor his own principal secretary, Bernard Roy, nor their staff, knew of the contents of this letter during the relevant period? If they were aware, why did they not tell him?

subtopic: KNOWLEDGE OF CONTENTS OF LETTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition says that the Hon. Minister remains under suspicion because of the ambiguous nature of the letter from Mr. Gorman. I think that is quite accurate. That is why the House has decided to take cognizance of this matter officially at 3.30 this afternoon. I am satisfied that at that time all appropriate questions can and will be asked and answered.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT OFFICIALS APPEAR BEFORE COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT OFFICIALS APPEAR BEFORE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House has not yet taken a decision on the matter and the committee has not been seized of the matter. The Prime Minister says that it will be referred to the committee. We will wait until that happens.
However, as we have said to him before in this House, that does not absolve the Prime Minister of his duties as Prime Minister to ensure the probity, credibility, and comportment of his Ministers. That is his responsibility and no committee of the House can absolve him of that responsibility.
Since the Prime Minister has refused to deal with these questions on the floor of the House, will he authorize the Secretary to the Cabinet and his own principal secretary to appear before that committee when it sits?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT OFFICIALS APPEAR BEFORE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, the committee is master of its own destiny. The committee can take whatever decisions it deems appropriate.
My hon. friend refers to the Prime Minister being responsible for the probity and credibility of Members and said that what transpired does not absolve the Prime Minister. I am not seeking absolution. That which transpired was straightforward.
My hon. friend was advised of the fact that subpoenas might issue in regard to an investigation undertaken under the Elections Act. Immediately upon being apprised of that, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stepped aside in the finest traditions of British parliamentary practice.
During the two months that the investigation and interrogations went on, he was outside the Cabinet. There was then a public statement issued by the gentleman conducting the investigation that no charges pursuant to that investigation would be laid.
It seems to me, in terms of reasonableness and fairness, that surely the hon. gentleman, not being charged, is entitled to all

February 2, 1988
Oral Questions
the presumptions of innocence which exist for all the citizens of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Is the Parliamentary Secretary now in a position to confirm first, that such a mission of Canadian Parliamentarians would be welcome in Haiti, second, that its security will be assured, and above all that its members will be entirely free to meet the main leaders of the Comite d'entente democratiquel

subsubtopic: DISPATCH OF PARLIAMENTARY MISSION TO HAITI- CONDITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer this question. It is clear that, before its departure, the security of the mission will be assured. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: QUERY WHETHER ARRANGEMENTS MADE TO HOLD TRULY DEMOCRATIC ELECTIONS IN HAITI

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to deal today with Bill C-84. First of all, if I may, I should like to repeat what many of my colleagues have already said. We are not debating this Bill simply as a fillibuster to paralyze the Government, but rather to make sure that the Canadian immigration policy is worthy of us.
Unfortunately, instead of educating Canadian men and women on this issue and eliminating the abuses of our immigration system, the Tory Government is going to the extreme. Last summer, the Government got scared and recalled the House to deal with an emergency situation. It was just an excuse, as we very well know, because Bill-84 has never been a priority of this Government. Since then, apparently, it has survived this wave of panic.
Mr. Speaker, the Government seems to be a little more flexible now concerning this Bill since a number of amendments proposed by the Standing Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs have been accepted by the Minister.
On the other hand, I should like to congratulate the Standing Committee for an excellent job and the unanimity which its members have demonstrated in their recommendations.
Although a number of amendments from the Senate Committee have been accepted by the Minister, other priority elements have not. Those are the points I should like to deal with today.
The first recommendation which was turned down by the Minister deals with the provisions of the Bill which would make it possible for a Minister or the Government to turn refugee ships around. Mr. Speaker, I feel it would be unfair to treat people arriving by ships differently from those arriving by planes. For one thing, they would receive a better welcome. How could a Government decide the future of people on the basis of their means of transportation? Contrary to the Bill, the Senate proposes to lead the ships into port rather than turning them around. This would make it possible for Canadian authorities to help genuine refugees on board while the captain would be liable to a fine or prison term for his criminal acts. This certainly would be a stronger deterrent. Indeed, I do not believe that simply turning a boat away will prevent traffickers and smugglers from trying their luck later. We therefore believe the Government should accept that recommendation. They could thus penalize the culprits and extend to people on board the legal safeguards provided by the Act, because actually, turning the boat away without looking at and assessing the condition of people on board is utterly inexcusable.
A second recommendation made by the Senate Committee was that we should not make it a new offence to aid or abet genuine refugees who do not hold valid visas. It is unacceptable in my view that we try to punish those who help people in need. Church people, priests or nuns for instance could be

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
charged with civil disobedience for helping people who are fleeing torture, threat and assassination in their home country. I would never have believed, Mr. Speaker, that this Parliament could enact a clause that is so offensive and backward. Canadians stated publicly they were ready to break the law if necessary to help those people who need such help. Such legislation is unworthy of us Canadians-people in Canada are much too fair and equitable to do that.
There is another problem in the area of security. Although the Minister stated a person is deemed to be innocent until proved guilty in our system of law, the Minister seems to take the opposite view when refugees are involved. The Government want to ensure that anyone who is suspect of being a security risk should be entitled neither to the refugee status determination system nor refugee provisions. I believe Mr. Speaker it is important to base ourselves on something more than mere suspicions under that system. We should not detain or turn back people on that kind of suspicions. Solid evidence is needed.
I would like to address another sensitive aspect of Bill C-84, that of search and seizure. The Minister stated he would like to have search warrants both in daytime and at night. He implies Senators opposed warrants being issued after 4 p.m. on the grounds that it was night time. But the Senate said nothing of the kind. It merely suggested it would be better if search warrants were issued during the day. Therefore the Senate recommendations will not prevent the Government from enforcing a warrant at night if conditions called for it.
Once again, the Government is going too far. Why provide for powers which could lead to abuses when our laws already show moderation, tolerance and intelligence? We do not want to take away from the Government the tools it needs to protect our boundaries. We want to improve existing mechanisms, but we do not want provisions which might violate the rights of Canadians.

We have never said that all those who claim refugee status are legitimate refugees. There have always been and always will be abuses. However, is that a good enough reason to punish the great majority of refugees who have legitimate claims? Why punish innocent people who have nothing to do with the ones who abuse our system? We have to try to be fair.
Canadians have always been proud of their refugee system, and it has evolved over a long period. Moreoever, our system is admired by many countries, even though there is room for improvement in our legislation. Our welcoming attitude to refugees can be cited as an example internationally. Why should we relax our efforts? Too many people are suffering hardship and need our assistance. Why should we close our doors to them, Mr. Speaker?
We know that Canada accepted over 60,000 Vietnamese some time ago, but that did not provoke a campaign against refugees and immigrants. However, it now seems that a single

I am quite willing for us to adjust the existing system, but let us do so logically and fairly. Canadians should be informed about the issue. On the contrary, many of them do the work that most of us refuse to do.
The recommendations of the Senate Committee provide the means to make our system fairer and more equitable. We should consider these recommendations and accept them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal briefly with this very important piece of legislation which is now before the Parliament of Canada, Bill C-84.
Mr. Speaker, you are certainly aware that our Party is against this Bill which was introduced last summer by this Tory Government as a response to a tragic situation.

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
There was in this Bill a violation of human rights, a violation of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It was also a violation of the United Nations Charter. In fact, it is a very discriminatory and reactionary measure.
M. Speaker, we have before us now a few amendments which have been proposed by the Senate of Canada. I support these amendments because they would make of this Bill something better and more efficient for Canada.
It may seem unusual for NDP members to speak positively of the Senate of Canada. The Senate is certainly not a democratic institution. Its members have been appointed by several Prime Ministers such as Mr. Trudeau, Mr. Pearson, Mr. Clark and the current prime minister (Mr. Mulroney). As I said, this is not a democratic institution. In spite of that, the many senators who are clever and well intentioned have put together a Bill which is better than that of the federal Government.
[English)
I think more than any other Member of this House of Commons, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) has led a campaign against this very regressive and oppressive legislation introduced by the Conservative Government. Starting last August, at a time when I and others were on the special committee studying the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord, the Hon. Member was leading the fight against this repressive piece of legislation. It is very unfair to both legitimate refugees from many undemocratic countries, and to Canadians who help refugees. It violates the Canadian Charter of Rights and the UN convention on refugees.
I have not taken part in this debate before today. I was not part of the committee as I was tied up in other work of this House, like yourself. However, I understand that when the committee held hearings most of the witnesses were opposed to the sweeping nature of this legislation. 1 also understand that when the Senate held hearings, it heard some 37 different witnesses and all of them except the immigration staff criticized and opposed the Bill. After those hearings, the Senate committee made 13 different recommendations and those recommendations are what we are talking about today.
Like yourself, Mr. Speaker, my family came from other parts of the world to settle in Canada. In my case, my ancestors came from enlightened and very democratic countries; on my father's side, from Sweden, on my mother's side, from Great Britain. They, along with many other people, created this great country. One reason they came here was that Canada was very tolerant of different ways of life, different languages and different
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we have two official languages in Canada. We have several cultures. On both sides, it is a society which is quite tolerant. It is a true mosaic of people from the four corners of the world. Now, we have a mixture, a truly distinctive Canadian society.

I do not think it is in the traditions of Canada to have this kind of repressive legislation before us today. When the Senate made its recommendations, it talked about a number of changes which should be made and I want to commend those changes to the House.
Amendment No. 1 would clarify the purposes of the Bill as opposing clandestine entry rather than smuggling. This amendment goes in the right direction. It more clearly defines what the purpose of this Bill should be so that fewer legitimate refugees are caught in a trap, through no fault of their own.
Amendment No. 2 and amendment No. 3 restore the right of a person being accused of being a security risk to hear the case against him or her, except where the judge decides that that would endanger national security or the safety of persons. This is a very important amendment with respect to civil rights or civil liberties. A person accused of being a security risk will have the right to hear the case being made against him or her. Without that right we are almost living in a police state. You can be accused of something and you do not have the right to hear what it is of which you are being accused. Innocent people can be caught in that net and be denied refugee status where they would normally qualify as legitimate refugees.
Amendment 4, which talks about the right of claim to refugee status, restores the right of a person accused of being a security risk to have his or her refugee claim determined nevertheless. This would live up to Canada's obligation under the U.N. convention relating to the status of refugees and entitle the person, if deported, to United Nations assistance in finding a safe country other than the one which he or she had fled.
While on this particular topic, I remember stories of a shipload of Jewish people coming to Canada from Germany in the late 1930s before I was born. They were to land in Montreal but were turned back by Canadian officials. That was a different time and perhaps a slightly different issue, but I think it indicates the consequence of lack of tolerance, the consequence of people being unable to explain their case, and the consequence for people who did not have a fair hearing in this country. They were sent back and many of them met their death in Nazi Germany.
It is very important that the legislation before the House today be drafted in such a way as to ensure that people coming to this country as refugees are not sent back to certain death in the countries from which they have come en route to Canada.
Amendment 5 deals with ships which are turned around. It requires that a ship suspected of bringing in illegal refugees be brought to port in Canada and that the occupants be dealt with in accordance with Canadian law. It is very important that they be dealt with in accordance with Canadian law. It is my understanding that amendments to this effect were moved in the committee by the spokesperson for our Party, the
February 2, 1988

Member for Spadina. There are violations of the Canadian Charter of Rights, of some pretty fundamental justices and liberties, in the Bill presented before the House.
Amendments 6 and 7 deal with aiding and abetting. They restrict these clauses by targeting only those who intentionally encourage false refugee claims or who assist clandestine entry into this country. This ensures compliance with Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This is an effort to target more effectively those people who intentionally encourage false refugee claims. This is an effort to target people who intentionally abuse, corrupt, and destroy the system for people who legitimately come to this country because they face persecution in their own country.
Amendments 9, 10, 11, and 12 deal with search and seizure and forfeiture. They ensure that search and seizure and forfeiture are allowed only on reasonable grounds and with reasonable procedures in keeping with Section 8 of the Charter of Rights. This is a very important series of amendments which would harmonize this legislation with the Canadian Charter of Rights and the Canadian Constitution as they affect those who live in this country. I do not think that is asking too much in terms of the amendments which the folks in the other place are suggesting to the House of Commons.
Finally, Amendment 13 would provide for independent review of the detention of persons held for identification or security purposes. This would ensure compliance with Sections 7, 9, and 10 of the Charter of Rights.
That is a very quick summary of the 13 amendments being suggested by the other place. 1 argue that those amendments are not radical but very reasonable. The ladies and gentlemen of the other place are not usually known as radical or revolutionary people. They are usually considered fairly moderate and sometimes rather conservative. They are noted for their sober second thought. Usually when they recommend something to this House their recommendation is made after a great deal of consideration and usually with tremendous moderation. If the Senate, after hearing witness after witness, church group after church group, and civil libertarian after civil libertarian, can make these kinds of recommendations, then surely to goodness the House of Commons and, in particular, members of the government Party can accept these recommendations from the Senate of Canada to improve Bill C-84 which is before the House today.
I would like to remind us all that this country has a very tolerant past. This country has been very generous and benevolent. This country was built by people of many lands coming to Canada and working together to build a tremendous society and a tremendous country. We have two great languages and many great cultures. These people together have built a great country along with the indigenous aboriginal people who were here before peoples from other parts of the world arrived.
This piece of legislation would turn back the clock. It is the kind of legislation you would expect from President Reagan in
Immigration Act, 1976
the United States or Margaret Thatcher in Great Britain, but it is not the kind of legislation you would expect from the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada with the history which it has had.
Throughout its history of leaders, from Sir John A. Macdonald to John Diefenbaker, the Progressive Conservative Party has been very progressive with regard to refugees, immigrants, or building a society based on tolerance. It is only the most recent Conservative Party members who have tried to turn back the clock on the progressive tradition of that Party which now forms the Government of Canada.
I am sure that if John Diefenbaker were in the House today he would be making speech after speech about how regressive, conservative, reactionary, and restrictive this Bill is. Mr. Diefenbaker was from my home Province of Saskatchewan. He built his reputation on defending the underdog, on standing up and fighting for the rights of ordinary people who were being discriminated against, on fighting for ordinary Indian people and for the right to vote, for decent lives, and decent services. John Diefenbaker would not tolerate for a minute this kind of reactionary Bill.
I also suspect that many in the Cabinet, if they were Prime Minister, would not tolerate such a Bill as is before the House today. I am sure that if the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) were the Prime Minister of this country or the Minister in charge of immigration he would not be introducing this Bill in the House today. I noted that he is not returning to Manitoba to seek the leadership of that political Party there. Therefore, we will not have to grant refugee status to Mr. Filmon. That aside, I am sure that if the Minister of National Health and Welfare were the Leader of the Party or the Minister in charge we would not have this regressive Bill because he is more in the tradition of John Diefenbaker and progressive prairie populism.
I ask the members of the Conservative Party to join with us, the Liberal Party, the Senators, the people of Canada, and the churches of all faiths, all of whom have said that this Bill is much too regressive. This is not the Canadian tradition, it is not the Canadian heritage. If we had this kind of philosophy many years ago we would not have in Canada many of the Canadians we have today.
I want to conclude by reminding people that over the years we have taken in people from many very regressive regimes.

Mr. Speaker, I know there is a great deal of oppression in the world. There is a lot of that going on in Africa, for instance, and one example is the present situation in Zaire, a political dictatorship where human rights are violated. Zaire is the former Belgian Congo. It is one of the great countries of Africa, where there is now a lot of discrimination against a large number of people.
There is also discrimination in Haiti. President Duvalier was a dictator as his father was before him, but now, although he is

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
no longer in Haiti, the situation is such that human and civil rights are non-existent. There was a phony election in Haiti where the principal candidate was not even part of the process.
There is repression in Haiti and there is also the situation in Central America, where in many countries, people who were strongly in favour of a democratic system and freedom of expression, association and rest, are now confronted with a repressive situation. There is also the situation in South America, in Chile. Several years ago, I remember we had a meeting here in the parliamentary restaurant with Mrs. Allende. Her husband was the President of Chile and had been democratically elected, and after only a few years, he was assassinated. Now we have a repressive regime in Chile, Mr. Speaker. We often meet men and women who want to come to Canada to live under a democratic system and start a new life. We are not the only country with a humanitarian tradition in this respect. There are many others. Nevertheless, I hope Canada will remain open and maintain its traditions and heritage. 1 hope it will maintain its humanitarian system for all refugees throughout the world.
I urge my friends in the Conservative Party to remain true to the traditions of John Diefenbaker and many other "progressive" Conservatives, to stand up for civil rights and civil liberty and make sure that the Bill that is passed by the House of Commons respects the Charter of Rights in this country and respects the United Nations High Commission for Refugees.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what you have just witnessed is an interesting exercise on the part of the Government to improve this piece of legislation six months after it was introduced as an absolutely urgent matter which required the recall of Parliament on August 11. We are now dealing with what would seem to be the final stages of the debate on this Bill in the fourth year of the Government.
Six months after the Bill was introduced, the Government still finds it necessary to rush in on a Tuesday afternoon to present amendments that it deems to be necessary through a delayed acceptance of suggestions that had been made to the Government both by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) on behalf of the Official Opposition and by the Senate. Perhaps this is an indication that at this rate, in another six months, we might have a piece Of legislation that will be acceptable to Canada and in accordance with the the basic principles contained in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
It is a sign of immense incompetence on the part of the Government that we are here, six months later, struggling along with a piece of legislation which could have been passed in a matter of weeks if it had been introduced with measures that would not be, in most legal opinions and in the judgment of refugee communities, repugnant or could not be eventually challenged in the higher courts. That would have made this whole exercise unnecessary and even a farce. That is the basic point.
I imagine it really upsets most Canadians to hear backbenchers of the Tory Party rising during the period preceding Question Period to lament the fact that this Bill is still being debated in the House. That is the highest level of hypocrisy accompanied by incompetence that has been witnessed in the House for a long, long time.
A few minutes ago the Minister of State rushed into the House to introduce two technical amendments, at least what he thinks are two technical amendments. But he admitted in his own words that they are in part a reply to the suggestions made by the Senate. That is an admission that the Bill is still far from being the type of Bill that ought to be leaving the House in order to command the respect of the Canadian people and the respect of our courts.
What we have here is an exercise in incompetence for which only the Government can be held responsible, not the members of the Opposition for debating it. We are not compulsory speakers in the House of Commons. We do not come here just to speak in order to see our name in print the next day in Hansard. We come here when we are hot under the collar, as we were in August of 1987 and as we are six months later today because we still find that some measures in this Bill are offensive.
The Senate has performed an outstanding role in examining Bill C-84 in its traditional and thorough manner. It has come to the conclusion to which Senators of all Parties, which in this case means Liberals and Conservatives, have agreed upon. Not one Conservative Senator disagreed on the package that has been sent to us here today for debate-not one. That is the reality.
The Senate is unanimous in saying that this Bill still needs to be amended. Yet some back-benchers of the Government, which is so-called Progressive Conservative, have the nerve to get up to complain that we are still debating it. We have to debate it because of its contents. What the Senate is saying is that this law must be improved on a number of fronts. Other speakers before me have already outlined them. I am not able to say something that is new on how the recommendations of the Senate run. They cover a wide range of clauses, and others have done better than I have done. The fact remains that there is here a principle to make laws that are good and that cannot and should not be challenged in higher courts. The Hon.
February 2, 1988

Member for York West made this point, as have others. It is an important point.
We want to make a contribution to the debate on this Bill in a manner that will achieve two things. One principle is that we want to ensure that our immigration laws are not abused. There is unanimous consent to that. The second principle is that we want to pass a law that will not be challenged in the higher courts and that will not therefore slow down, almost impede or bring to a grinding halt the whole legislative implementation of the laws that the House is debating right now. We are trying to improve the quality of it now so that it will work later on. That is the point.
The nature of the amendments is quite clear in the submission of the Senate. In his intervention a few days ago the Hon. Member for York West dealt with them in a very clear manner. He put on the record his thoughts with respect to turning back a boat, something which the Government wants in the present legislation as proposed.
The alternative we are advancing is that, instead, the law be such that it permit the Minister to escort these boats into port. That is a sound and convincing argument. I recommend that Hon. Members read page 12303 of Hansard for January 26. At that page Hon. Members will find the intervention of the Hon. Member for York West who said that the Senate articulated the recommendation that rather than turning back a boat it be escorted into port. We think that there are some very basic good and solid reasons for doing that.
If we want to punish the smugglers of human misery, as the Hon. Member for York West pointed out, then we should bring the boat into Canadian harbours and confiscate it, sell it and punish the captain by imposing a fine upon him or by placing him in prison. Why does he say that? Because this is a lesson which will not be forgotten for a long, long time. That is the reason. In doing so the word will spread on the international circuits among potential captains and boat owners that when one comes close to Canadian waters or touches them then they are in for a rough time and that one may lose one's shirt. Is that not the point? Is that not the reason we want to do it?
For the life of us it is very hard to understand why the Minister of Immigration cannot see the merits of this measure that was proposed, expounded and advanced by the Opposition back in August and again put forward and advanced by the Senate as a whole. It is extremely difficult to understand why this is not being accepted.
On January 26 the Hon. Member for York West concluded with this observation. He said that the discouragement is greater if we bring the boat in and then punish the culprits. He pointed out that we would be more wise since we would be able to question the captains. He also pointed out that we could try to break down the rings and the networks that are operating throughout the world. These are three solid and good reasons which the Hon. Member put forward. Why turn back the boat? This is something that escapes our ability to understand.
Immigration Act, 1976
Another point made by the Senators, which deserves our attention, has to do with the question of punishment of those who aid and abet refugees. You have heard it I suppose, Mr. Speaker, more than you would like to, and I do not envy you. It is your task to hear at times things over and over again. Your Honour has heard some pretty solid arguments in the House and in the Senate about the notion that the law should not punish organizations and individuals who help refugees.
It is more than individuals and organizations with whom we have to be concerned. I say that because in the offices of Members of Parliament in many cities in the exercise of our daily duties we inevitably come into contact with people who are here as potential refugees. They come to our offices seeking advice. If we were to deal with them, we could be in breach of the law as proposed now. There must be a dozen Members of Parliament in the House now who, over the years, have spoken or been spoken to by individuals who would like to be considered and accepted as refugees and who have been helped with information and advice. All of a sudden when this law is implemented anyone who in the future comes in touch with and offers advice or answers to a person who would like to declare himself or herself as a refugee in Canada might be in trouble with respect to the law.
That is not a fair measure, and it is not a measure that can be considered lightly. I notice that on the same day the Hon. Member for York West made a reference to Nancy Pocock from the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees in dealing with this issue. The present Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) says that he has to reject the notion that this particular clause be deleted from the Bill, and in his release he states that this amendment would constitute a reversal of the policy upon which the Immigration Act of 1976 was based. That is incorrect. It is not so. The Immigration Act of 1976 does not advance the notion in this forceful and authoritative manner that it does now that anyone who is involved in assisting and in dealing with refugees is in breach of the law. Otherwise, I think many of us would have been in trouble a long time ago.
Instead, what we do support on this side of the House is the amendment by the Senate which would limit criminal prosecution to those who intentionally encourage false claims, and to those people who assist clandestine entry. That is a line that has been drawn by the Senate, which is a very fine line and a very important one. It deals with false claims, and it deals with the matter of clandestine entry. I think that that would be safe ground and also fairer ground on which to base the spirit and the operative part of the proposed legislation.
On those two grounds alone there is reason enough to rise in the House and to speak out. There is still time for the Government to accept these interventions on our part. At the rate that the Government is doing so, it may be some time before this will happen. Until then, Mr. Speaker, all I can say to you is that it is not right for the Government to blame us for the fact

February 2, 1988

that a Bill introduced in August is still here. There are Bills which travel through the House fairly quickly and with a lot of co-operation. If this Bill is still here after six months the only one that can be blamed and ought to be blamed is the Government and those who propose it.
