I would like to commend the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for his reassuring words, words that we heard from him only a few short months ago when this debate was present before this very Chamber in the hot days of summer. His interest perhaps was not only derived from the two boatloads that arrived on our shores, but certainly that interest and passion emanates from long and hard work during the 1970s and early 1980s when he was a very active member of the standing committee on immigration at that time.
The Hon. Member for Davenport correctly pointed out that there is a certain amount of hypocrisy when members of the Government rise during Statements Pursuant to S.O. 21 prior to Question Period and suggest that somehow the Opposition is delaying and filibustering this legislation, and that this emergency Bill is still very much alive in our Chamber as of February, 1988.
As was pointed out in part by the Member, the truth is that this question and the report from the other place that we are debating today did not come exclusively from Liberal Senators, but it was endorsed unanimously by all Senators. In fact, some of the Senators from the government side were more passionate and emotional in the disdain in which they held this piece of legislation, and that triggered a number of discussions, perhaps behind the scenes as well as in front of the committee with the Minister, that helped this report and allowed the Government to recognize that it did go too far.
At no time did the Government push the Senate committee to deal with it more quickly. At no time did the Government ask its Senators on the government side to expedite matters, as they did in the committee. Therefore, there was not the political will or the political necessity for that to happen. Now that we have had the time to reflect over the several months that have elapsed since the summer, I think the Government got the message that it had erred, that this Bill was overkill, and that Canadians were looking at this in a progressive and moderate manner, something that the Government was not doing.
In addition, Members of Parliament from the government side have also been debating this Bill. Government Members have also been standing up and asking questions. This is a debate. It is a discussion. If we are not to discuss and debate in this Chamber, and if it is not for the Opposition together with members of the Senate, including government Senators, to try to push this Government a little more close to some degree of progressivity, then who should do so?
On that note, I wish to ask the Member for Davenport what are his thoughts, in terms of the whole question of leadership and being at the leading edge of educating and coming to grips
with this very emotional yet significant issue, rather than simply waving hands and calling those people illegal migrants and suggesting that somehow Parliament has to come together because there is an emergency and impending crisis. The Hon. Member was a member of this Chamber and a member of a preceding Government that had the example of the Vietnamese boat people and partnership between community and Government at its best, but in addition to that there were other programs that complemented that particular exercise. What does the Hon. Member think of a Government that can and is able and wishes to lead and create a country in a direction that is better for humankind and for the international phenomenon of refugees, as opposed to a Government that runs from the issue, looks at the polls, and has the knee-jerk reaction that we saw in the summer months?

The example of the boat people is a very good one. On the over-all question of leadership, this afternoon, February 2, six months after the introduction of this Bill, we were treated to the spectacle of the Government rushing in and asking that this Bill be given two additional amendments. After this Bill had been introduced in August of last year, debated on second reading, sent to committee, having heard all the witnesses, having heard the views of the Opposition, having it reported back to the House of Commons, having debated additional amendments, having a debate on third reading, a discussion in the Senate, hearings in committee of the Senate, receiving it back from the Senate, the Government is still thinking over and wondering what to do to improve this Bill after six months.
Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker? What an immense sign of incompetence. It is not even a question of leadership. It is a question of not knowing how to run the business of the nation. That is what it tells me, if on February 2 the Government has to rush into the House with two amendments to a Bill which was introduced six months before and after all the phases of hearings and debates on the amendments.
It would be nice to be able to discuss leadership. The Government does not have the faintest idea. We find incompetence in the way it managed the trade negotiations with the United States. We find incompetence in the way that it dealt with the United States on acid rain. It is an empty cupboard. We also find incompetence with regard to toxic chemicals in the Niagara River. The Government is in the fourth year of its mandate. If its Members were to think back to 1983, they would find that if they managed to do anything in this Parliament it was because we prepared the ground for action in a number of fields.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate in the debate on the government motion in relation to Bill C-84.
As all Hon. Members surely remember, in the middle of our summer break we were summoned back to Parliament to deal with a national emergency. The national emergency at that time was that a boatload of people were entering Canadian waters and in fact had arrived at our shores seeking refugee status. This became quite a topic during the summer months, and the Government immediately called Parliament back to deal with the matter. It stated at that time that a real national

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
emergency existed and that it required proper legislation right away to deal with the perceived threat of waves of would-be refugees coming to Canada.
Here we are well into the new year, 1988, and we are still debating a Bill dealing with that so-called grave national emergency.
Part of the reason we are still dealing with the debate at this stage, and why the Opposition has been so concerned about it, is that the legislation the Government introduced at that time was so seriously flawed that every group in the country which dealt with questions regarding refugees was opposed to what the Government was doing. Amnesty International, the Canadian Bar Association, church groups, and humanitarian groups from coast to coast were raising serious concerns about the legislation. The Canadian Bar Association raised legal concerns. It felt-and it still feels it today-that despite some of the amendments which the Government has now allowed to its original legislation, the legislation is so seriously flawed that the courts will have to throw it out. It contravenes our Constitution and its Charter of Rights.
The Canadian Bar Association claims that in numerous instances in this piece of legislation proper due process will not be provided to people who come to our shores and attempt to land as refugees. The church groups also point out that what this legislation does is to destroy the tradition we have been trying to build as a haven for those who seek to escape political, religious and racial persecution in their home countries. While we as Canadians take some pride in our image of being decent, caring people, it is certainly true that in the past we have committed what I would call acts that besmirch that image. Members, particularly colleagues of mine in the New Democratic Party, have raised during this debate the case of the group of Indian refugees who came to Canada around 1914 and who were sent back to India. Some died at the hands of the Government of India of the day. We all know of the case of the ship St. Louis which, with around 900 European Jews trying to escape what they knew was coming in Europe, set forth to find a safe haven across the Atlantic. They were turned back by numerous countries, including Canada. They returned to Europe and very few of those 900 European Jews survived. They were caught in the Holocaust and died in Nazi concentration camps. That situation was something that we as Canadians could have prevented, except that our political prejudices and fears at the time entered into the picture and we denied people access to Canada.
It is not with total pride that we as Canadians can look at our record. We have to recognize that we have made mistakes in the past, mistakes that have cost people's lives, people who otherwise would have made a tremendous contribution to our country and the well-being of it. Instead, our own prejudices at the time made them face certain death. Let history ensure that we do not make the same mistakes again, that people who seek
entrance to our land, many of whom are not white Anglo-Saxons but Hindus, Pakistanis, blacks from Africa or people trying to escape from the insanity of the Middle East, are welcomed into our country. Let us make certain of that because history will also judge us as we judged the Liberal Government of the day which turned back the boatload of European Jews.
The Government called us back last summer in order to deal with Bill C-84 and this great national emergency as the Government described the situation. The Bill has too many overtones of what the Government did in 1938 when it turned back the boatload of European Jews. There are too many overtones of racial and political prejudices here.
What we are debating today is the Government's response to the Senate. I know you are aware, Mr. Speaker, that I have no great love for that institution called the Senate. I think a non-elected body of essentially politically motivated people, a body consisting of political appointees, should not have the power to prevent legislation from passing. Unelected people, while they definitely play a role in a legislative process, should not have the final say in things. They do have a role to play and I think the Senate has played its role in its report on Bill C-84. 1 would never stand here in my place and describe the other place as being filled with men and women who are wild-eyed radicals seeking to undermine the security and the well-being of the Canadian state. I do not think I would ever describe hon. Senators in those terms. That is why I think the recommendations which the Senators have made through amendments to the Bill surely must be seriously considered. These are recommendations made by men and women in the other place who are concerned about the security and well-being of the Canadian state but who are also concerned that proper due process is followed, that we maintain our international commitments signed with the United Nations, and above all, that we live up to our commitments found in The Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Hon. Senators have pointed out, as members of the Canadian Bar Association and various other legal experts have, that Bill C-84 is seriously flawed. It contravenes our commitments to the Charter of Rights. It contravenes our commitment as a society to due process of law, and it contravenes our international commitment to the treatment of refugees. As such, it is sad indeed that the Government on the whole has rejected these well thought out amendments which the Senate in a unanimous report has passed back to this House. Not even Conservative Senators in the other place rose and objected, argued or voted against these recommendations, not one Conservative Senator.
We come back to the questions of where is the crisis, where are the solutions. This Bill is certainly not an acceptable solution. Most probably the courts will strike down the Bill. What are we doing here debating this Bill? Is it the concern of the Government to push this Bill through? I suspect that first and foremost the decision made last summer was for political reasons. The Government now would just like to pass this Bill,
February 2, 1988

make it into law and have the courts overturn it, and that some future government can set about enacting a law that is workable, reasonable and compassionate. The Bill we have today will not do that. I suspect the Government is not very much interested in this matter anymore. Hopefully, in its own thinking, the Government has fulfilled its political objectives last summer when it tried to appear tough. A political knee-jerk reaction existed last summer. I do not think that speaks well of the Government. The Government lost faith and credibility at that point, and today we are cleaning up the mess.
I can stand here and read into the record various quotes from individuals. I could put on the record the words of the executive secretary of the Council of Christian Reformed Churches. 1 am certain that the Hon. Member for Surrey- White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) would be aware of that gentleman because many of his constituents belong to the Christian Reformed Church. In a telegram dated January 27, 1988, that gentleman said this:
Government motion on C-84 inadequate and unacceptable relative to
Canadian Charter and UN Convention. Senate amendments apply. Please
enact these.
We see the limitations of this legislation. We see the incompetence with which the Government has handled the situation. We saw the political knee-jerk reaction last summer which brought us back here, and seven or eight months later we are still debating the issue. We will end up with a mess which I suspect will make us a laughing-stock the world over.
It is not that Members of Parliament have failed to point this out to the Government. The Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, the majority of which is made up of Conservative Members, reported to the Government, but that report has not been acted on. In fact, the Government has done the unprecedented and refused to respond to the report. Government Members themselves are not happy with this legislation and recognize its faults. Yet the Government is still insistent on continuing with it.
The Senate made several important amendments and I wish to touch on those briefly in the few remaining moments of my time. One of the important amendments in essence ensures that in the process to determine who is a security risk, those who are found to be a security risk cannot be precluded from making a refugee claim. This is important because the original legislation does just that. Without that opportunity, many of these people will be sent back to their place of origin where they could very well lose their lives.
Another important amendment deals with turning ships around. Under this legislation when the Government and its agents suspect there is a boatload of would-be refugees in international waters, it can send the Navy out there and turn that boat around and prevent them from landing. That notion has some serious flaws. First, there might be some genuine
Immigration Act, 1976
refugees on board. Their only means of getting to this country is through this kind of exercise.
Second, if we are concerned about trying to stop the unscrupulous from exploiting immigrants, let us say in Europe or other places, by selling them tickets on an old boat to come to Canada illegally and sneak into the country, you want to get them into port so you can seize the ship and arrest the crew. That is how you stop those illegal enterprises which exploit immigrants and would-be refugees. You do not just turn them around somewhere on the high seas. That does not make sense.
Third, most illegal immigrants come here not via boat but via air. Certainly we are not going to turn airplanes around in mid-air.
Another amendment which I think we should support deals with the question of aiding and abetting refugees. This is a silly part of the legislation. The Government is making it a criminal offence for anyone to help a refugee who does not possess proper papers, a visa, and so forth. For heaven's sake, in most cases people who are genuine refugees are escaping from their countries because they face physical threats from the established authority. They are not going to get exit visas. Yet we would make church and other humanitarian groups liable to criminal prosecution if they aid refugees. Surely that is crazy. There are many other parts of Bill C-84 that just do not make sense, and I suspect the courts will strike them down.
You are indicating that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker. I hope I have been able to enunciate some of the areas of concern I have about C-84, and I certainly wish to entertain questions at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member finished his well thought out speech with a prediction which matches the evidence that both the House and Senate committees studying the Bill received from expert legal testimony, that this Bill will be struck down by the courts. We are not talking about one clause which is more or less controversial. We are talking about a variety of clauses which are very questionable from a constitutional standpoint and that of the Charter of Rights.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member what he predicts will be the response from the Canadian public to this situation. We have to keep in mind that the Government is trying to promote this legislation as a cure-all, the answer to the problems in the refugee determination system. However, if it is struck down by our courts, not only will we be unable to see a resolution of the problems, the situation will become worse than it is now. We will have a paralysis of policy. What does the Member see as the problem for the Government, which basically will have misled Canadians and ushered Parliament to pass legislation which contravenes the number one law in this country-our Constitution?

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, December 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Nickerson that Bill C-211, an Act to amend the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this Private Members' Bill, I understand that it is an issue in which my northern colleague has had some interest for a number of years. Having read all the background debate and considering what the Hon. Member is proposing, 1 must say first that while I appreciate that the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation may not serve the interests of some northern fisheries as well as he would like, I find it difficult to support this particular Private Members' Bill. Let me explain why.
One of the problems is that this corporation deals with a vast geographic area including Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories. Therefore, there it probably has some difficulty in working as effectively for all regions as it might. However, I cannot agree that a Bill which would do away with the essence of that corporation would indeed solve the problem. That opinion was obviously shared by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Binns) who also felt that while there might
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
be some serious issues that could be redressed by the corporation, this Bill would not serve to do so. He felt that eliminating the mandate of the corporation would not serve the interests of any of the regions with which it dealt.
Unless there has been a change since the beginning of 1988, neither the provinces involved nor the Governments of the Territories have requested a change to this Act. Therefore, support for this Bill would be unilateral, without having the concurrence or involvement of the other jurisdictions in drafting changes they would like.
As someone from the northern territories, it seems we are always raising the issue about being consulted and playing a part in the drafting of legislation which affects us. Therefore, certainly the consultative procedure that should take place in any changes to this corporation is very important.
While the Bill attempts to address certain problems, I am not sure they concern the corporation. In my view, the problems relate more to such issues as the distances from markets in many cases, which result in great difficulty in selling products that originate a long way from the market. I suggest that changing the corporation process does not mean it will change the price that buyers will pay for the product. Since the markets now utilized by the corporation would be exactly the same as those of the independent fisheries, I fail to see how changing that will necessarily make for a better system for the fishers. The primary concern is how we can sustain the industry and make it better.
A very interesting edition of Northern Perspectives of November, 1987, dedicates an entire issue to Arctic fisheries and the need for some new approaches to Arctic Fisheries. I want to mention a couple of points made in some of the articles. For example, one article informs us that in the northern territories particularly there is a large supply of fish which are underutilized in the inland fishery and that it is the high cost of production relative to the market-place that limits the development potential. I know from my own region that there are many production problems. More processing on site would effectively increase the marketing potential. A fishmarketing corporation does not necessarily impinge on that.
Another article which addresses Arctic fisheries points out that many of the limitations on the development of Arctic fisheries has not been with respect to supply or the availability of markets, but on the investors' estimates of profitability. In other words, if the investors do not think it will make money they will not invest, which is understandable. We want to develop those markets and we believe that there is a potential for them, but we suggest that this will not be accomplished by doing away with the essence of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
Several recommendations have been made by the Senate committee. Indeed, I believe that one major initiative is now taking place, which will hopefully address some of the problems at least for the northern and Arctic areas. These are problems which the Member for Western Arctic (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
February 2, 1988
Freshwater Fish Marketing Act
Nickerson) knows firsthand, some of which he knows better than I.
The draft fisheries policy now being prepared by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Arctic marine conservation strategy which is being disseminated now by the Government for discussion, really provide the kind of framework for the study of this issue and for the utilization of fisheries products in consort with development, conservation issues and economic development aspects.
I believe this would be one of the most effective ways to address some of the issues of northern fisheries in particular, without taking the more heavy handed method, as 1 see it, of attempting to change the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act which may have a negative effect for those other sectors that the corporation serves under that Act.
I believe there are consultative processes now in place that may very effectively address some of the problems which the Member has attempted to address with this Bill. For that reason, 1 do not support the Bill. I believe there are many more effective ways to address the problems in this area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during this debate I have been accused many times of persistency. Some people have even gone so far as to describe that as obstinacy. For that i make no apology because it has been my observation over many years in this place that persistency pays off, especially when you have right on your side, and know' that what you are doing is right and will benefit the people of Canada. In those circumstances I have found that persistency pays off in the end. i am sure it will in this case.
Since this Bill has been under debate we have heard the voices of reaction raise up. We just heard one from the other side. The Hon. Member who just spoke did not let her lack of knowledge of the fishing business interfere with her ideology.
The Freshwater Fish Marketing Board has been doing quite a lobbying job because it has a lot to fare in this issue. It has a rather cushy deal going for itself. The fishermen must sell to the FFMC at its prices. It has no competition and is beholden to no one. It has been trying to protect that rather cushy deal and has been doing much lobbying. It has even got some fishermen to sign papers saying that they are not in favour of this Bill, can you believe that? The people who did that were on the fishermen's advisory committee. They are put there by FFMC people themselves. We know what side their bread is buttered on.
I have not heard any real argument against this Bill. Everyone on the other side of the House has said that if this
goes through, it will gut the FFMC. It will not. The FFMC will still continue to exist, but this will make it competitive.
If we can agree with a Crown corporation like Petro-Canada, and some of us do and some of us do not, we can agree with having a Crown corporation in competition with other companies in the petroleum business. There is nothing really wrong with that. It keeps Petro-Canada relatively honest-not entirely honest but relatively honest. In this case, though, there is no competition whatsoever. There is nothing by which to judge the FFMC in this area. There is in the other part of Canada that is not under government monopolistic control, the Great Fakes area where there is free enterprise and business is just a-boomin'.
I would like to say a few things that are of special interest to fishermen in the Northwest Territories. First, I would like to read into the record a telex sent by Mr. D. R. Stewart, the President of the Northwest Territories Federation of Fishermen. It was addressed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) here in Ottawa. The text reads as follows:
This is to inform you that our N.W.T, Federation of Fishermen strongly
support Dave Nickerson, our M.P., concerning his Bill C-211.
There, Sir, you can see that the fishermen of the Northwest Territories support this issue in its entirety.
In the Northwest Territories, there are special concerns, there is no inter-territorial market to speak of. We cannot sell fish locally in any quantity. It has to be exported.
There is a speciality product in the Northwest Territories. The quality of the fish, especially for smokers, is far superior to that found in southern lakes, and it should be marketed as such. It should be marketed at the premium prices that premium quality fish should command.
We have to get our fish directly to market. The way it is now, it is first caught on the lake, hauled in fresh to the plant, frozen, shipped to Winnipeg and kept in a warehouse in Winnipeg for six months or a year. Then we try to sell it to someone, but no one wants to buy that kind of fish. That fish ought to be on a table in a restaurant in Fos Angeles, Chicago or New York the day after it is caught. The Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation cannot see that. However, there are people who are willing to make the investment in this business so that that can happen, but they cannot do so because the FFMC is blocking their way.
We suspect that northern fish is used to subsidize southern fish. The argument goes like this: The FFMC says, "You want some of that good quality northern fish? Before you get that, you will have to take some of the inferior stuff'. I have every suspicion that that accusation is correct.
To give credit where credit is due, some of these things have been recognized by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. He has promised to consider the possibility of exempting the Northwest Territories from the monopoly. It only provides about 10 per cent of over-all sales of FFMC, so when this Bill
February 2, 1988

gets into committee after second reading, that is something that can be looked at.
1 would like to look at the principles involved in this matter. The principle contained in the present Act is that the freedoms of individuals, whether they be fishermen, dealers in fish or retail or wholesale merchants, are restricted. We should not do that, but we have in the case of these people. Their freedom and liberty has been restricted by an Act of Parliament.
I know that in the North and in many provinces, we can have a viable fishery. It is something that can be commercially operated at a profit and everyone can do well from it, just as they do on the Great Lakes. However, there is the Government's view that it is some kind of social scheme. People are administering grants, but we do not need to give grants or subsidies. We need to open up the markets and let the Fishermen sell the fish to those new markets for the high prices it will command.
In this country, people should be free to take up the profession of fish dealing if that is what they want to do. It is unthinkable to me that we should restrict anyone from going into that profession.
Finally, I want to bring to your attention, Sir, the great debate that is occurring throughout Canada on liberalizing trade. There is a big debate about the elimination of unnecessary restrictions to interprovincial trade, whether it be in beer, wine or any other commodity. We have entered into a free trade agreement with the United States. We are looking at removing restrictions under the GATT. Let us do the same thing for freshwater fish. Let us have liberalized trade in fish. Let a fisherman have the opportunity to sell his fish to whomever he wants. Let us pass this Bill at second reading stage so that it may have the further consideration in committee that it deserves.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard in relation to the amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, and on the motion of Mr. Lewis:

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to enter this debate again on the basis of the motion the Government tabled earlier this afternoon. The first part of the motion deals with the technical definition of the term "exigent" when a warrant does not have to be obtained by immigration officials in their search of any records, documents or premises.
The Government has now amended the clause so that the word "include" reads "mean". That obviously makes more precise the definition of the word "exigent" so that it clearly means circumstances in which the delay necessary to obtain a warrant under subsection (1) would result in danger to human life, safety or the loss or destruction of anything liable to seizure.
I think it should be pointed out that our Party's position has been to suggest that warrants ought to be obtained in the same way they are obtained under other aspects of Canadian law. As we stated during the debate, we believe that the Government tried to go too far. It has tried to make Immigration officers into Rambo-like creatures who would go across the country and on mere hunches and suspicions enter and ransack any premise to confiscate any document without good cause. It was our position therefore to try to bring some moderation and some clarity to the situation and to have the Government recognize that the provisions by which individuals obtain the necessary search warrants is a system that is working and working effectively. At the same time it protects those rights and privileges that we have as citizens.
We accept this part of the motion in so far as it defines more precisely the circumstances under which a warrant would not be authorized or asked for, that is to say, in the case of life and death and perhaps lots of important materials. This part of the motion grew from discussions in the other place when it was deliberating this Bill in committee. It began as a point raised by Liberal and government Senators alike. Perhaps it is the

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
fruition of the sober second thought which some Members of the Government have called into question. This is a clear example, as is the report of the Senate, from which we will derive benefit. It is a by-product of democracy at work.
The second part of the motion introduced by the Government only a few short hours ago is the more important of the two. Under the legislation which is before us a Minister would have not only the power to turn back the boat, something with which we disagree vehemently, but he would have this power as well as being able to delegate it to his officials and other immigration officers. Our position throughout the debate has been that to turn back the boat is incorrect. It is incorrect on a number of grounds.
The Government must recognize that any boat coming in would not have on board a cargo of wheat or a cargo of steel. We are talking about boats coming into our waters carrying human cargo. There are human beings on board these boats. Obviously and logically there should be some procedure by which we can ascertain who is on board and how many people there are. We should be able to ascertain what are the ages of the people on board and the condition of their health. We should know from where they are coming and if they want to make an application in the process that is offered.
One of the reasons we have argued that the boat should be brought into port is that it is a human response to human beings who deserve at the very least our attention and due process. In this way there will not be a double standard by which people coming in by boat will be refused access into the refugee system and those arriving through our airports will have full access to that system. What we have suggested is that turning back the boat would not only disallow due process to human beings but it would also create the unfortunate situation whereby the mode of transportation will dictate the treatment which a potential refugee will receive.
That is simply unacceptable. If we have one way of proceeding with one refugee application, then the response to all applications should be consistent. It should be uniform. We cannot allow a piece of legislation to say, in effect, to one applicant, "You came in by plane. You are allowed to make a refugee application. Here is the paper and there is the office". We cannot then say to another would-be applicant in the same breath, "You have come in by boat, therefore you do not have the opportunity to make an application". However, it is most likely that that person will not even see the Canadian shores. Thus it is wrong from a human perspective. It is wrong from a procedural perspective as well. It is also wrong from the point of view maintained by this Party that such a provision will not realize the premise or the objective of the legislation which, in the Government's words, is to discourage abuse and to stop manipulators trafficking in human flesh.
We have argued that if we really want to discourage these traffickers then one does not do so by very weakly turning back the boat. Any captain smuggling human beings would obviously have cash on delivery. He would have the money
even before his passengers were on board. Therefore, any captain will say to himself, "Well, I have a 50/50 chance. There is a 50 per cent chance that 1 will get into the country and a 50 per cent chance that I will not. Therefore I will simply go out a little further, dump my cargo overboard or bring it to another part of the Canadian coastline, perhaps undetected, or even deposit these human beings on someone else's shore in another country". It really does not make any difference to the captain because he will have collected his profit already.
We have suggested, as has every single witness who came before the legislative committee of the House of Commons as well as those who appeared before the Senate committee, that if we want to discourage these kinds of traffickers, then for goodness' sakes let us escort them into port. Let the Coast Guard officials bring them into a port of our country. Let us discourage any would-be smuggler from ever coming into Canada again by making a clear example of the captain and the crew that we have under supervision. Once we have them in port we will be able to prosecute such individuals under the law. If they are found guilty, then they can be fined or imprisoned. We can also confiscate the boat and sell it if the individual is found guilty.
We have said that that would send the clearest and strongest message to any other captain who might be loading a boat to make a similar run. If the news were to get back to a port that a captain was fined or he and his crew were imprisoned, that his ship was confiscated, then I believe that that would discourage others from leaving for Canada. Yet if the captain of a second boat heard that the worst thing that happened to the first crew was that they were simply turned around, then I think that that captain would proceed.
We have suggested that if the Government wants to convince Canadians that it wants to stop abuse, then it must follow up with procedures that will allow one to realize that goal rather than playing and indulging in public relations gimmickry which does nothing to discourage people. It somehow satisfies the appetite of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who can say to Canadians, "We are turning back a boat," as if that would really buy him the popularity which he seeks.
On the strength of the testimony received in committee, we in the Liberal Party believe that Canadians are much wiser than the Government gives them credit for Canadians will understand, as I have understood, that there are ways of discouraging abuse and further trafficking, and that turning back a boat does not in fact do that.
By having the crew and the captain in our port, we will be able to interrogate those people. We will ask them, "How much money did you charge? How was it organized? Who else is involved? How extensive is the ring? Where else does the network plan to hit? When? How many people?"
February 2, 1988

Therefore, as a country we would be much wiser and have at our fingertips more information with which to combat and stop the disgusting network of human beings taking advantage of serious situations in the world, and trying to strangle the individual into coughing up their last dollar saved in order to give them misleading information about the promised land.
If we were able to bring the boat in, as a country we would be one step closer to breaking down this illegal, immoral human trade. Yet the Government wants to wash its hands of the whole matter and turn the boat around, as if that would allow us as a country to protect ourselves better. If the boat is turned around, who is to know that the next day another boat will not dock in Vancouver, or the day after in Toronto?
If we send a concerted message that we will deal with those people in the harshest manner possible under due process of the law, and if we send a message that we want to break down this network and get at the epicentre and paralyze it in order that this business would come to an end, then we will be respected. People will say that Canada is taking serious action to stop this type of business. They will be looking for other markets but not Canada.
This would also send a message to other countries and our allies that this is the answer. If Canada imposed this type of tough response, and if that was complemented by other countries doing likewise, then we would be able to overcome this problem on a world-wide basis, rather than having countries turning back boats only to see different boats landing at different times in their country.
How many times can the Government recall Parliament in the middle of the summer and get away with it? How many times can the Government create a crisis? How many times can a progressive and important policy such as the immigration policy afford to be undermined by a Government that is not serious about stopping the problem that it talks about?
Therefore, we are saying that now is our window of opportunity. Now, when the public has focused its attention, because there are many competing issues, is the time for Parliament to deal with it swiftly and correctly rather than in a number of years having Canadians say, "I thought you took care of that. Parliament was recalled on an emergency. You passed legislation that you told us would solve the problem". What is the Government going to tell those Canadians, and why it did not pass the legislation that it should have? In a sense, we are trying to avoid a problem that I envision if this legislation goes through.
The specific motion before us again came from deliberations in the other place. It came from discussions with the Minister and with his staff at committee and after committee. In the report, Senators, including Senators from the government side, vehemently opposed the concept of turning back the boat. But they said that if the Government is to persist with this clause, if the Minister is inflexible, as he was during the summer months, at the very least the power of turning back a boat
Immigration Act, 1976
should be vested solely in the Minister and/or his Deputy Minister.
As the legislation presently stands, it would allow the Minister to delegate this very regressive power to various deputies and officials of the Immigration Department. In its wisdom, the Senate decided that, if this clause is not removed from the Bill, which it hoped the Government would do, then at least the authority under which this can happen should be restricted.
1 believe that that amendment proposed by the Senate and introduced today is the lesser of two evils. We hope that in the dying days of discussion here in the forum of the House of Commons before this Bill gets sent back to the Senate, the Minister and the Government can reach out for the consensus that exists in the House and across the country to change this clause. 1 am hopeful still that the Minister will extend the flexibility that he has shown in recognition that they have erred in a number of important clauses, in order that when it goes to the other place they will have one less thing to worry about.
In the likelihood that they do not, I believe that the House should approve the idea suggested by the Senate that the power to turn back a boat only be vested in the Minister and his Deputy Minister. First, because it is a power that should not be taken lightly. We should not have an immigration official in Nova Scotia, Victoria, or Toronto making that decision. The Minister might not be there. He might be in Cabinet or have other pressing matters to deal with. Immigration officials should not be allowed to make a decision that can affect human beings.
We are suggesting that, if anyone, the Minister should at least be the one to say yes or no to turning back a boat, not only because he is the most important official of the entire Department, but also because he would be politically accountable for what would be a very important decision. Any official out there could be lost in the woodwork, could state that he or she is not politically responsible to the House of Commons, they were doing their job, or there was a communication breakdown. We do not want those excuses when we might have human blood on our hands. At least let us make this decision politically accountable to the electors of this country, as it should be.
From the vantage point that the decision would be very important, we believe that this amendment would be worthy of the support of this Chamber. In closing, I hope that this will not be made necessary if we change the clause regarding turning back the boat, as suggested by the Senate report.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to explain what has not been dealt with until now by the Government's motion and by the comments of the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi). I fully agree with the comments made by the Hon. Member. I would like to add a couple of comments of my own on each point.

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
The first part of the motion is:
That of Bill C-84 be further amended in Clause II by striking out line 2 at
page 13 and substituting the following therefor:
""exigent circumstances" mean circum-"
In other words, on page 13 we have this section: "For the purposes of subsection (5)", which is the one going before, "'exigent circumstances' include circumstances in which the delay necessary to obtain a warrant under subsection (1) would result in danger to human life or safety or the loss or destruction of anything liable to seizure". What they are talking about is subsection (5) in Section 103.02. This is a general section which allows officers to seize a boat or to seize anything, and subsection (5) says that an immigration officer or a peace office may exercise any of the powers referred to in subsection (1) without a warrant, if the conditions for obtaining the warrant exist but by reason of exigent circumstances it would not be practical to obtain the warrant.
My Party and I do not agree with this section. We think it is excessive, and therefore we do not agree with this subsection. However, since our objections have been overridden by the Government and Parliament, and the objections of the other place have been overridden by the Government, there is this one very small change to which the Government has agreed and with which my Party and I agree. In other words, it is a question of limiting the scope of this subsection which says that they can take the action without a warrant if there are exigent circumstances that would not make it practical to get a warrant.
The way they had written it first was broad enough to drive a herd of elephants through. They said that exigent circumstances include circumstances in which the delay necessary to obtain a warrant would result in danger to life or safety or destruction of anything liable to seizure. Now they limit it to say that exigent circumstances mean those circumstances. They cannot use any other circumstances. If they cannot prove that delay to get a warrant would result in danger to human life, or that it would result in danger to human safety, or that it would result in the loss or destruction of anything liable to seizure, anything that they have a right to seize; if they cannot prove one of those three points, then of course they cannot act without that warrant.
It seems like a very reasonable point, and I am glad that the other place pointed out the utter folly of opening it wide open by saying: "Well, it just includes those reasons, but of course a judge would have to say, if the question came up, that it could go far beyond those reasons". This is a small improvement on an otherwise bad clause, but the clause is going through, so I am glad to have the damage limited a little bit in that sense.
The other part of the motion is more important. It reads:
That the Bill be further amended in Clause 16 by striking out line 16 at
page 24 and substituting the following therefor:
"82.1(2), 83(1) and 91.1(1), and any such power,".
Standing by itself of course that does not mean anything to anybody. However, when we look at page 24, we find that this is the section which gives the Minister or the Deputy Minister the authority to delegate their power to officials of the Department and, in the middle of a long paragraph that delegates that power, there are certain exceptions made, certain actions for which the Minister or Deputy Minister are not permitted to delegate their power. Only the Minister or the Deputy Minister may do the things listed here. There is a number of them, but in the line we are dealing with it is 82.1(2), 83(1), and now they are adding 91.1(1). In other words, this limits the authority of the Minister to leave an important decision to a lower official.
When we turn to 91.1 we find that it is in fact a very important decision. This decision, 91.1, is the decision to turn back the ship. I think all the people who have spoken against this Bill, either when it was in the House or when it was in the other place, would agree that this is a good amendment.
The clause itself is an outrageous one, as has been said by everybody who has spoken to this during the past-half year and more, except of course for the Minister and his officials. They are the only ones who defended it. The clause says that the Minister has the power to turn back a ship at sea.
I won't repeat what I have said in the House, what many others have said in the House, or what the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) has just said. I won't repeat how bad that clause is, but bad as it is to have the danger to the passengers, bad as it is to have the failure to punish the captain, this amendment can limit the damage that would be done because only the Minister or his Deputy can do it.
Pardon me, I have been mistaken. It is not the Minister's Deputy. Only the Minister can do it. If the Minister believes on reasonable grounds that a vehicle within our territorial waters is bringing any person into Canada in contravention of the Act, and so on, he may, after having regard to the safety of the vehicle and the convention and the vehicle's contents, direct the vehicle to leave, and so on.
If that were left as it had been and any minor official could have that power delegated to him, and if there were disaster because of it, or if the law were made ineffective because people were turned away and slipped back again the next night, and if that were done by a minor official, the Minister could escape responsibility; perhaps fire the official but the Minister would escape responsibility and the public would have no real recourse, legal or political.
However, with this amendment nobody in the land except the Minister will be able to order a ship to be turned back. If the Minister does that, he knows that he will be subject to very close public scrutiny for what he has done. He knows that if the law is mocked because the captain just goes away and tries again, or he knows that if there is evidence that passengers have been harmed as a result of that turning away of the ship, then he pays the political price for it as a Minister. He is
February 2, 1988

publicly accountable for what he has done either to the passengers or to the law in that case.
Therefore, I am sure that the Minister will be very careful about what he does. It is even quite possible that he may not use that power. Unfortunately, that still does not deal with the point that we have been making, that it will be better to arrest the ship or whatever is the naval term, or seize the ship at sea by the power of our Coast Guard or whatever we need, and the captain and the passengers, and bring them into port. If the captain is believed to have done wrong, charge him and try him according to the law, and the passengers should be dealt with according to our law as those who have come to the country. Perhaps some of them will have come without proper visas and so on. Perhaps some will claim refugee status.
That would have been a much better way of dealing with it, but the Government has consistently refused to carry out effectively what it said last summer was absolutely urgent and necessary. It could have had that law passed through both Houses and proclaimed law last August if the Government had seriously carried out what it said it intended to do so, which was to enact a measure to discourage this kind of dishonest action by a captain. It did not seriously intend to do that. The public begged and urged the Government to do that, but it would not. That chance is now being lost by the action of the Government. Nevertheless, the folly and the potential active harm is limited because the Minister will know that he and no one else is answerable to the public.
There is one further piece of harm though, which even this amendment will not prevent. This law has already sent a contrary signal to many other countries and Governments in the world. There were Governments, especially in the southwestern Pacific, which had been turning ships away. The Vietnamese boat people ships, in particular, were turned away, let go adrift at sea, and they were pushed off the beach. Canada was in the lead of the western countries which rebuked them for that and said the action was inhuman. Civilized people do not treat boat people like that. We urged them to stop the practice. We even offered at that time to take the burden of some of those refugees. The United Nations High Commission for Refugees was very thankful for Canada's strong voice saying it is wrong to turn ships away at sea.
Now Canada has said, according to the Government, that it has changed its mind. Canadian people, to whom the Nansen Medal was awarded, have not said that. Every public delegation and every non-departmental delegation which spoke on this spoke against turning away the ships. But the action of the Canadian Government now sends a message, whether to the Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia, to Singapore, on to whoever it is in the southwestern Pacific, saying that Canada has reversed its position. It is now decided that civilized nations like Canada can and will turn ships away at sea.
Immigration Act, 1976
The misfortune is that even if the Minister, or perhaps another Minister who follows him or has more sense than this Minister, never applies that clause and never turns a ship away at sea, the example is set by that clause, by its adoption in this House last year and by the motion that the Government wishes to have adopted now. It is a very destructive one and will seriously damage the whole work of refugee protection throughout the world, not just in Canada.
I regret very much that the Government has been so hardhearted and willing to contradict the stand that Canada took as recently as two years ago over the wrongness of turning away ships. But at least, as I say, the potential damage is now to be restricted by this amendment. I would assume that the House will be adopting the last motion unanimously.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe I have spoken yet on the main motion. I do have some matters that I want to raise as a result of my own experience and what I have learned from Canadian history on this issue.
A little study of Canadian history shows that Canadians for about the last 200 years have aided and abetted people on numerous occasions getting into this country who claim to be and turn out to be refugees. There were a few-there will always be some who get through the net for a while-who turned out not to be refugees. Our history tells us that Canadians without or in spite of the federal authorities'
approval have helped refugees. That has occurred on countless occasions in our history even before Confederation.
People who came to this country in its earliest days were escaping from dictatorship, privation, starvation, imprisonment, and constant fear for their lives. I suppose what we call a refugee today would not be the same in the terminology used then. However, they were refugees of some kind from regimes under which they could not live in peace and with some degree of security and opportunity. Over the years hundreds of thousands of Canadians have gone to extraordinary lengths to help those people without the support or approval of federal authorities. I think about the underground railroad from about 1850 to the middle 1860s when churches and individuals aided and abetted the smuggling into this country of blacks from anywhere and everywhere in the U.S. It was smuggling, in many instances, at great peril to both the smuggler and the person being smuggled. In those days they did not suffer the approbation of the federal authority or what passed for any kind of immigration appeal board. No one in this House would now denigrate or decry the efforts made by those people in that operation.
Let us come to later years. I remember as a youngster in what was then and is still called today a white Anglo-Saxon Protestant family, hearing the grown-ups talk about all those bohunks who got into this country during and following World War I right up to the beginning of World War II. Those people came here from many parts of Europe in the 1920s and 1930s. Thank goodness! Some of the children and grandchildren of those so-called bohunks occupy this Chamber. Had we a law in place such as is proposed by the Government, they would not have made it.
We were called back here on August 18 for a so-called national emergency. Some 157 people showed up in a boat off the coast of Nova Scotia. Did the people of that province rise up in arms and say "You cannot let these people in"? No, they welcomed them, made them peanut butter sandwiches and tea and coffee and gave them shelter. That seems to me to be the state of mind and attitude of the people of this country. Yet the Government reacted with the typical 19th century mindless, inconsiderate attitude which has existed among many previous federal Governments in this country going back well over 100 years, to our everlasting shame. I suppose it is because of that everlasting shame that so many Canadians remember and do not want to repeat the same errors of omission and commission.
A boatload of Sikhs arrived off the shores of this country about 80 years ago. It caused an uproar. Our national authorities said those people could not be admitted. They had been escaping oppression, some of it under British colonial rule, and of course some 80 years ago we were still something of a British colony. There was much official approbation about allowing these Sikh refugees in, and refugees are what they would be under today's terms given the conditions under which
February 2, 1988

they were living 80 years ago. About 30 years later a boat carrying over 900 Jewish refugees arrived off Canada's shores. We turned them away.
There are some very old teachings in Christianity about sanctuary. It applies even to our actual physical church buildings in which one can seek sanctuary. Sanctuary can take a variety of forms for a variety of reasons. I think this country was victimized by what could at best be called panic button pushing last August because 157 Tamils arrived off our shores from Sri Lanka, via West Germany, or anywhere else. The response of the Government with this legislation flies in the face of the activities of hundreds of thousands of Canadians for something over 150 years, the provision of sanctuary. They provided succour in aiding and abetting those people to enter Canada. Three or four generations later many of their great grandchildren and great great grandchildren are honoured citizens of this nation. To bring in a law in this day and age that makes people who are active in helping refugees from many nations guilty of aiding and abetting the entry of those poor souls into our nation flies in the face of our history and I strongly and profoundly believe flies in the face of how most Canadians sincerely and strongly feel about this matter.
Of course, there will be a few, a very small few, who will abuse and misuse our generosity, our humanitarian instincts, our traditions, and our history. There will be some, no doubt about it, but 1 would rather take a chance on the few who would abuse our hospitality and sanctuary and err than penalize the vast majority who are entitled, under all the international agreements to which we are party and under our own history and activities as Canadians for over a century and a half, to the fullest consideration under our law.
Our law has gradually become more generous as time has passed. For many years we have been generally in concert with the United Nations Declaration on Refugees and Human Rights. We have been ahead of most countries, even with some, and behind a few others. However, generally speaking we have a reasonably good record. I think that is mainly because the overwhelming majority of Canadians do not want to repeat the terrible acts of omission and commission carried out by governments of the day in previous times in our country.
I do not think any Hon. Member of this House wants to be a party to retrogressing to the attitudes and states of mind which prevailed on earlier occasions. Surely we can do no less than to extend the fullest process to anyone and everyone who comes to our shores claiming refugee status. Our laws must provide to the fullest extent for complete hearings, even when there is doubt, just as we treat our veterans of four wars.
If there is any doubt, the benefit of the doubt goes to the veteran. If there is any doubt with regard to those who want sanctuary in our nation but we cannot prove differently under the rule of law, the benefit of doubt must go to the person to
Immigration Act, 1976
whom we are giving sanctuary until they themselves, by their actions and deeds, prove otherwise. Surely that is the least we can do in a society which claims to be civilized and humanitarian, which claims to adhere to international agreements and treaties.
I am endeavouring to be non-partisan because 1 think there are many people of all political stripes in this nation who feel as do you and I, Sir, about the people who seek sanctuary, who are escaping from things about which our forefathers knew but which we do not comprehend. Our forefathers were able to get here by one means or another, and I like to think that the generations in this Chamber and the generations out there younger than us will remember that because they learned of it from their parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents.
Everyone who came to this country since 1982 could, I suppose, in the vernacular of the day when I was a child, be called bohunks regardless of from which country they came. My grandfather came out of the pits and mines in Wales. He was poor and ended up working on the CPR tracks in the interior of British Columbia in 1902. I suppose you could call him a white Anglo-Saxon bohunk, the terminology which we used in reference to people who came from central and eastern Europe in the twenties and thirties and the fifties and sixties. It is interesting to study history and consider who the people are who make up this nation, from where they came, and what they contributed.
In the name of humanity, in the name of Christian ethics, in the name of mankind, even if we err and let some slip through the net who could be terrorists, I would rather err on that side than take a chance of excluding 156 of 157 Tamils who are not terrorists and do not have a criminal record. I would rather take a chance on a handful slipping through and taking advantage of our system than condemn thousands and thousands by withholding from them a Christian, civilized, and democratic right to sanctuary, decent treatment, and the fullest benefit of our laws and society.
The Government has risen to temporary and so-called public opinion against people who would abuse our system to get ahead in the line-up. There are ways of correcting getting ahead in the line-up. You do not stop the whole darn line-up just to satisfy a small minority in this nation who have some ancient, archaic, and out-moded idea about the purity of the Canadian system. If it were not for the contribution to this country by people of every race and religion known to mankind, our nation would not be as good as it is.
1 ask that the Government go back to the drawing board and reconsider what it is doing. I am the last one in this Chamber to express any sympathy for the other place. I have been one of those, since I was much younger, who believe it should be abolished, that it is an anachronism of the 19th century. However, I will give members of that place credit, along with many Members in this Chamber, for standing up against a bad piece of legislation and for trying to make a bad piece of

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
legislation better. I hope the Government will accept that and accept many of these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, this is my first opportunity to debate the main import of the motion that has been proposed by the Government. I want to support the comments made by the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) in expressing regret at the fact the Government has decided to prolong the sitting of the House tonight rather than carry on as normal.
I am concerned about that because 1 think this is bad legislation. Rather than listening to what the Senate and people from this Party and the Official Opposition have been trying to tell the Government, it is determined to barrel through. While 1 do not know its agenda, it seems to want to barrel through with a proposal that will prove unworkable, unconstitutional, that will ultimately sour relations with many countries in the world and certainly offend many well-meaning Canadians who are concerned about Canada's role as a safe haven for victims of oppression in different parts of the world.
Let me remind the House that the kind of efforts that have been made to scare Canadians and make them paranoid about refugees coming to this country are entirely unjustified. There has been absolutely no evidence that people who have claimed refugee status to come into Canada have turned out to be threats to the national security of this country. In fact, it is remarkable the degree to which refugees who, having found a safe haven, have settled down to become productive members of our society, often under difficult circumstances because of the difference between their homeland from which they were forced to flee and this country.
This legislation is reprehensible because of the degree to which it will make Canadians criminals. Even if the Deputy Attorney General is required to sign a process against people who are deemed to have been assisting in the illegal entry into Canada of people claiming to be refugees, most refugees apart from those who are well heeled financially are probably breaking some law. They arrive here without papers from their home country because of an oppressive Government that will not give them travel documents or permit them to leave the country legally. If they do not have travel documents they cannot get a Canadian visa.
If they went to a Canadian high commission or embassy in their home country they would immediately be marked by the secret police of a dictatorial government in their homeland as someone trying to buck the regime by leaving. We saw the example of a person in El Salvador who sought a visa and was subsequently killed by the death squads before she was able to leave and come to Canada with the Canadian permit she was able to get. The act of seeking the paper was enough for her to become a marked woman and, as a consequence, she was killed.
Canadians who respond to that kind of situation will be subject to prosecution. Whether or not that prosecution takes place, nevertheless it will have a chilling effect on those Canadians who may wish to reach out and seek to give sanctuary to people coming in.
February 2, 1988



Mr. Speaker, I have had some experience in these matters, because during the sixties I was directly involved in a program to help Americans who were refugees because they were dodging the draft in their country during the war in Vietnam.
Mr. Speaker, some of these Americans were risking very severe penalties, because they were already enrolled in the Armed Forces and subsequently deserted to come to Canada. Fortunately, the Secretary of State for External Affairs at the time, Mr. Mitchell Sharp-in fact, I discussed the matter with him recently-had established at the beginning of the two World Wars, when Canada was at war with Germany and the United States had not yet entered the war . . . What did the Americans do about Canadians who left Canada to go to the United States, after breaking the law in this country and deserting from the Canadian Army? The United Stares took them in. Mr. Sharp decided that in this case the Government would do likewise.
Nevertheless, when I was helping these people who challenged U.S. policy, I was uneasy, even if I was not breaking the law. When I went to the border to help someone cross the Canadian border to enter Canada legally, after they had first entered Canada illegally as visitors intending to stay in Canada, I was worried. It was a scary experience.
Now suppose we tell priests and members of religious communities and all those people who want to help: You will be subject to severe penalties. You will be committing a crime by helping refugees. In that case, the safe haven now afforded by Canada will disappear.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote the Senate Committee's report where it says, in summarizing the testimony given by the vast majority of witnesses who appeared before the Committee, and I quote:
All of the witnesses before the Committee agreed that abuse of our immigration laws must stop. However, they pointed out that the drastic measures in this bill will not affect only those who would come to abuse our refugee system. For example, any person approaching our borders without proper documents-whether, engaged in a fraudulent scheme or fleeing from persecution and danger-would be subject to the same measures.
So here is the problem, Mr. Speaker. A Canadian who helps and provides a safe haven for one of these refugees may incur sanctions under the Criminal Code of Canada, no matter whether the individual has gained fraudulent entry into Canada or whether he will simply not flee from persecution and danger.
This individual might be detained for a month without his case being the object of impartial review ...
Now it would be seven days.
If he was engaged in resistance against the government of the country from which he fled, he might be detained longer and described as being a security threat.
No change, Mr. Speaker, and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service might decide that this individual who claims refugee status is indeed a threat against the security of a government. Then one of the reasons why this individual fled
Immigration Act, 1976
from his native country is that his security was threatened and the government of his country treated him as if he was a threat to the security of the country. Had the individual been engaged in resistance against the government of the country from which he escaped, he could be detained much longer and considered as being a security threat here in Canada, never mind the fact that there is no proof that these refugees-as a class-who came to Canada, and we did welcome hundreds of thousands of refugees over the past forty years, are a threat to Canadian security.
Again I quote the Senate committee:
Canadians who assist people arriving in Canada without the necessary documents would be subject to prosecution, including those doing humanitarian work by looking after refugees, the very field of activity where Canada has gained international recognition.
Mr. Speaker, our international reputation will be tarnished as a result of Bill C-84.
As well, I am worried that a lot of what we are talking about is not necessary. Earlier today, I pointed out that there was a consensus that had emerged about how Canada's refugee determination process could be tightened up and accelerated so that false refugee claimants would very quickly find themselves sent back to their homelands at great cost. They would have paid refugee or immigration counsellors, they would have paid for their flights, they might have sold their farms or businesses but then found themselves a month or two later on their way back to their homelands, much the poorer for the experience of having tried to enter Canada by declaring themselves refugees and having their claims determined to be unfounded.
Word gets out pretty quickly. There would be articles in the press and electronic media in those counties indicating that 200 or so refugee claimants were returned from Canada. The message would pass through the village market-places, the cities and towns, the clubs and sporting events, "Do not try to come to Canada if you do not have a case". We would very quickly see that particular source of refugee claimants dry up. People would no longer try to avoid the rules or jump the queue in that way.
In addition, I think we need to be talking quite seriously about the whole question of immigration levels. We know that Canada is one of the most desirable countries in the world. In many ways, it is even more desirable than the United States because Canada has a much better network of social security and because people see that this country does not have the negative downside which is the underside of the American dream.
Could I ask for order, Mr. Speaker, from my hon. colleagues?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was saying that I am very concerned about the whole question of levels of immigration. One of the reasons people have tried to use the refugee process rather than normal immigration channels is because those normal immigration channels have been plugged. Levels of immigration are far below the targets set every year. The targets themselves are inadequate. Net immigration for Canada is far below what we need for the potential we have in this country. Frankly, with the potential Canada offers, I believe that we ourselves are in danger of giving offence by not bearing our share of those persons who wish to come here.
The immigration policy is now putting so much emphasis and person power on encouraging entrepreneurial immigrants that the brothers, sisters and friends of the people who live in my constituency who do not happen to have those advantages cannot get into Canada. Some of them wind up saying they are refugees because that is a way they have found to get into Canada when they cannot come in the front door. I am afraid that that is one of the realities of the situation now.
If we could just take some of the resources that go into the refugee process and use them to encourage, in a way that is fair and open, the necessary increases in immigration and in services to immigrants once they have arrived here, we might be in a healthier situation than the one we are in right now. Unfortunately, the Government has not been prepared to do that. As a consequence, we have instead Bill C-84.
I must ask myself what in fact is the agenda the Government is pursuing. It is trying to make Canadians believe that there is an absolute fleet of boats waiting to come to Canada, so they will cut it off. The total number of boatloads of people seeking to come to Canada in the life of this Government has been two.
Whether it is Sikhs from India or Tamils from Sri Lanka, there certainly is a case for considering that those persons may in fact have some legitimate claims as refugees. Those claims can and should be determined quickly so that if people are
eligible to stay, they may stay, and if they are not eligible to stay, they will be sent back to their homelands.
It is worth noting that Punjab in India which I visited last March is in a state of governor's rule, rule by the central government, and there are some dreadful atrocities taking place there. It is a very unhappy place. We know that the Indian Army has been involved in Sri Lanka and as well there have been acts in Sri Lanka which appear to be violations of human rights directed against the Tamil population. There is a war-like state in portions of that country because of the situation between the Tamils and the majority population. It is not necessarily easy for any of us to reach a snap judgment and say, "Well, anybody who is a Tamil coming into Canada is obviously not a refugee, or anybody who is a Sikh coming into Canada is obviously not a refugee". To some extent that depends on the rules and on their interpretation which is why we have a refugee determination process.
It is clear that situations change over time. For example, a Palestinian who sought to come into Canada as a refugee six months ago might not have been acceptable at that time. It might be that under the refugee determination rules which are in force now Palestinians seeking to enter Canada today would be considered eligible since conditions have changed in a regrettable way in the West Bank and in the Gaza Strip. I do not know. I think we need to have some kind of flexibility about all of this. If it is felt that the level of refugees coming into the country is totally excessive, then I believe we have to consider that. But that is not the case now. We are talking about perhaps 10 per cent at the most of the total number of immigrants coming into Canada. I believe that is a tolerable level for a country which has been as open hearted as Canada has been.
I just had some new cards printed up for use in my constituency. They state, "Member of Parliament, depute, deputato", which represents three of the linguistic groups in my riding. They are also in Vietnamese, Chinese and Arabic. We know the situation in Lebanon which is from where most of the population of Arab origin in my riding come. We know the situation in Vietnam and that so many people fled that country to come to Canada as refugees. It is worth noting that a significant number of the Chinese who are now here in Canada were also refugees either from Vietnam or in certain cases from the People's Republic. This is the ethnic mix in just one central city constituency.
My forebear back in the 1820s was subject to oppression by the British who brought Protestants into Ireland to take the best land. They sucked the country dry at the time of the Great Famine. In the 1840s Ireland was actually a net exporter of food. Yet the people were starving to the point where the population fell by 1 million or more in the course of 10 or 15 years. Eventually, my ancestor had a fight with his landlord and came to Canada the next day. The rest of the family followed. They made a great contribution to Canada.

When 1 was a young boy growing up in Toronto in the 1940s there was talk that I deplore about what were called displaced persons, DPs, refugees. The Reichmanns might have been considered DPs or refugees. Frank Stronach, the owner of Magna International, might have been considered that as well.
I asked myself if someone had helped Frank Stronach into the country, would he or she now be subject to the penalties that are to be found in Bill C-84? The answer is quite probably yes.
If someone like Frank Stronach came today from Africa or from Asia and could not obtain direct transit to come into the country or could not afford it, then could he come into Canada as a refugee under this Bill? The answer is no. That is why when the vote is taken tomorrow my colleagues and I will oppose the Government's rejection of the Senate amendments on Bill C-84. I plead with the Government to review the situation to try to make a decision on the basis of consensus rather than on the basis of confrontation.
