Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), who has a great deal of experience in his constituency and in some of his previous work in the matter of immigration. I think his comments are quite relevant to the basic problem that is before us.
One of the points that he made is that this Bill is likely to offend many other nations. I can think of various ways that it might offend either the nation from which refugees come, the nation to which a ship is returned, the nation owning the ship or other nations which are concerned with helping refugees.
I am wondering if the Hon. Member will explain a little further. I know that he is actively concerned with matters concerning the external affairs of Canada. He has been on parliamentary delegations and visited places such as India. Can he tell us what he thinks will be the offensive impact of Bill C-84 on some of the other nations with which we have to deal, whether they are nations in the western hemisphere, Europe, Africa or Asia?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) for his question. 1 would say that we are talking about two groups of nations. One group will be delighted at this legislation, or will at least tend to support it. The other group will be offended.
Which are the countries which will be delighted by this legislation? I think that General Pinochet will be delighted by it. I think that General Mobutu will be delighted that Canada will not serve as a haven for refugees from his oppressive regime in Zaire. I think that President Botha of South Africa will be pleased with the legislation which, among other things, may make it harder for members of the African National Congress to come to Canada. I could go on and on in terms of citing repressive and oppressive regimes around the world which, if they notice what Canada is doing, will note that for once Canada is lining up with their views of the world and not with the view that has been traditionally taken by Canada.
Immigration Act, 1976
Who will be offended by this legislation? I think that groups such as the Red Cross in Geneva and world-wide will be offended by it. I think that Amnesty International, which has been fighting for human liberties and rights around the world, will be offended by it. I think that the various Helsinki watch groups, remnants of which still survive in parts of the Soviet Union and some of the eastern European countries, will be offended by it. I think that those countries at the United Nations which have looked to Canada to provide leadership in the field of international human rights will be deeply offended by this legislation. They will see that far from adding to the solution of human rights problems that Canada is in a small way becoming a part of the problem.
One of the most dangerous features of this legislation is the following. Canada, through Bill C-84, is setting a precedent which will reinforce certain countries in western Europe which have been unduly tightening their refugee legislation and which may encourage other countries that have not done so to do so in the future. In other words, legislation such as this feeds on itself. In other countries there are immigration bureaucrats who will say to their ministers or legislators, "Look, Canada saw that it had to bring in Draconian legislation, we had better do the same thing. Canada is turning people away. If we do not do something then all of the people that Canada turns away will come to us". We will feed paranoia rather than aid generosity.
There are a great many countries around the world which traditionally have been generous and looked to Canada for leadership. They will be offended by this Bill.

I believe that Canada has to make laws concerning refugees open and generous. We can afford to do that.

I have listened to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) and he has mentioned many things that I question. He stated that the western European nations are listening to their bureaucrats. He has not offered any proof of that, he has offered only a comment. I ask him to offer proof that the bureaucrats of western European nations are throwing true refugees out of their countries, and that the members of their Parliaments are listening to the bureaucrats.
1 am wondering what all Canadians are feeling, not what the world is thinking about Canada, and about how the countries of the world are asking if Canadians are doing the best for true refugees. Of course, we are. We are known for that. But we have to put a stop to those who are coming in here illegally, and those who are sneaking into this country. They have to bear the price of their follies, whether it is the fact that they paid too much money to get someone to sneak them into this country illegally, or whether it is the fact that they were stopped and asked, "Do we know if you are a criminal? Do we know if you are a person of good moral stature who should be living in this country?" We are a sovereign nation.
I would like to ask the Member for Ottawa Centre to comment on this, not from his point of view, but to sit back and answer truthfully as to whether he feels that the majority of the people of Canada are willing to let everyone in and hopefully no one will be a criminal, and hopefully no one will kill or do any harm to anyone in this country, but let us accept all of them, and hopefully we will eventually eliminate those who should not have been here in the first place.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I remind the Hon. Member that in my comments I pointed out that there is absolutely no evidence that people who have come into Canada as refugees and stayed here are security risks or criminals. There is absolutely no evidence of that at all. 1 would point out to the Hon. Member that the question of coming in as false refugees is a question on which there was agreement on all sides of the House. We do not think that thousands of people should come in from Portugal or Brazil because immigration counsellors have led them on and told them that there is a way that they can get into Canada.
We have suggested, together with the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, and Rabbi Plaut in his report, means by which those people could be quickly turned around and discouraged. The word would get back and very quickly that flow would be choked off. 1 do not believe there was a problem with that, except that the Government refused to listen to those particular questions.
When the Hon. Member asks whether I think that people who come illegally into this country should be turned back, he does not realize how far he is going over the line. It is impossible for a person who is oppressed in Central America or in
Chile to come to Canada with a visa and with all of the legal requirements. The bulk of legitimate refugees who are in transit around the world are guilty of some illegality or another because they could not move if they sought to act legally.
Therefore, the Hon. Member is saying, and with Bill C-84 the Government is saying, that all of those legitimate refugees will effectively be forced to endure oppression in their homeland because they will not be able to come to Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in the debate on Bill C-84 and the amendments put forward by the Senate. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) had an opportunity to correct some inequities in Bill C-84. For the benefit of those who are following the debate, Bill C-84 is the refugee legislation.
Mr. Speaker, the Bill now before us reflects the hard-nosed attitude of the Minister of Employment and Immigration who put it forward-it reflects his heartless character. And I will tell you how the legislation led to a couple of further actions by the Minister of Employment and Immigration that clearly prove his lack of understanding and his lack of a humane approach to problems.
It will be remembered that the same Minister of Employment and Immigration put a tragic end to the Katimavik program for the young. The Minister could have said: 1 am curtailing the program, but I am replacing it by something just as significant. But with his obstinacy, his whip-wielding, headmaster attitude, he turned a deaf ear on representations made by the young, Members in this House, even senators, and Canadians generally-he refused to do anything, with the definite purpose of showing who was the headmaster. He clearly showed that although he has an angel face and the outward look of St. Peter, he actually has a heart of stone.
The second remark deals with the second legislation and the Minister's behaviour toward workers, middle-aged workers hurt by unemployment insurance cuts. And no later than noon today, Mr. Speaker, in answer to my questions the Minister said he did not mind if a middle-aged worker that lost his job, for example with Weston and Hygrade, was not entitled to UI benefits because he was getting a pension-that it was all the same to him, there was nothing he could do. His mind is set, he gives nothing.
And today, on the refugee legislation he has the same attitude, the same rigid approach, a basic lack of humane approach to and understanding of individuals.
February 2, 1988

Mr. Speaker, it must be mentioned that we have been recalled in August by the Minister. The Government recalled Parliament in August because it believed a boat load of refugees was coming. It requested guns, planes, F-18's that went hunting over the sea for a ship that would be coming with ten people aboard. All they found was a way to spend taxpayers' money, to have us sit here in August, but he is no better off than before he put the legislation foward. This is nothing but a scenario for prodding the people so they would oppose and fear refugees.
Mr. Speaker, the people in Quebec and Canada are humane people. People in Quebec and Canada are generous. They proved it in the past, and they still are proving it today. Just as the Canadian and Quebec people, Members of the Opposition feel that we should try to stop the illegitimate refugees who are abusing the system. But we should make sure we deal with the real culprit. I suggest that the amendments proposed by the Senate made that possible. The approach of the Minister is, whenever he believes a ship has illegitimate refugees on board, he should order the ship to leave or not enter Canadian waters; according to the Senate's proposal, which is similar to that put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), who is doing a fantastic job on this issue, the Minister should say simply. Well, let us take this ship into port. Let us arrest and punish the culprit who has exploited these people. But because of his attitude, the Minister is jeopardizing the lives of the passenger by turning the ships around; the Government is waiting for someone to die in Canada or abroad to become sensible and change the legislation, as it did in the case of paternity leaves.
Mr. Speaker, it seemed to me that this logical, sensible and humane approach sought to discourage those who were taking advantage of people's kindness. Concerning the bill as introduced, my colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) was right to mention Nelson Mandela, a South African individual who is fighting to promote equality, eradicate Apartheid, a sort of racism based on colour ... As recently as this morning, during Jean Cournoyer's radio program heard in Quebec, someone mentioned that a person was treated like an animal because of the black colour of his skin. This individual would like to flee his homeland to come to Canada because his life is at risk. Well, the Minister of Employment and Immigration-not with the support, 1 am sure, of a great many Conservative Members who are people of conscience-would return this individual who does not meet the criteria. As a terrorist, he is unacceptable. Yet, it is only someone who wants to fight for his rights. If the Minister of Employment and Immigration had been faced with such a situation, he might have reacted more violently than Mr. Mandela did in his own country. Mr. Speaker, the problem with this Bill is that it does not make any distinctions in dealing with those who abuse the system and illegitimate refugees. It is like taking a canon to kill a fly in a room where there are 100 people. Everyone will be killed because of one fly, because of one little problem.
Immigration Act, 1976
There is another aspect. I believe that the Minister is determined to show that he is a proud man who does not give in to pressure, but in fact, he is gaining nothing. In real life, there is nothing to gain by thinking that you are right and everyone else is wrong, because the Official Opposition is not alone in denouncing the Bill introduced by the Conservative Government, and the Senate is not alone either. I believe that everyone knows that I do not hold the Senate in such a high esteem, but the Senators have played an important role in this issue and they are earning their pay. They are paid to study the Bills passed by the House of Commons and to return them to us. The Minister has to recognize that the Senators have done a good job because he was forced to accept amendments on points he had not noticed before. This shows that the Senate did a good job. Then, there are all the groups concerned, all the church groups, whether they are Catholic, Protestant or Orthodox, all the pressure groups, all the people who work closely with refugees, because a refugee is not someone who has just won $100,000 in a lottery. He does not behave the same way as other people. He is fleeing his country because he is being threatened. He might have suffered for years. He might have seen his father and mother getting killed, he might have children, brothers and sisters, but he was able to escape.
We are not talking about someone who happens to teach the children of the Prime Minister. If someone else than Mulroney had been elected, that teacher would not be here. But as he teaches the Prime Minister's children, he has his papers. However, he was not being threatened in France. A refugee is someone who has to use desperate means and rely on other people who want to help him. I read in the speech made by my colleague that if such people succeed in escaping by boat, they will be refused and returned to their country of origin. However, if they succeed in finding a plane, it is a different matter and their claim will be considered. Have you ever seen such stupidity or such a double standard? "If you are a good refugee, you will come by plane, but if you are a bad refugee, you will come by boat."
Before pushing this Bill through, I believe that the Minister of Employment and Immigration should reconsider in view of the three major blunders he has already made, first, as concerns young people by cancelling the Katimavik program, then in the case of older workers by cutting back unemployment insurance benefits, and now in the case of refugees. With respect to immigration and refugees, I think that he should heed to the advice and listen to the suggestions and comments of my colleague for York West (Mr. Marchi). I think that in his comments, recommendations and claims my colleague is advocating control measures. Of course, he is suggesting an approval, but also some assistance and more humane measures instead of shooting or striking the first ones to arrive on the spot. The Senate has proposed or recommended that those who are really guilty should be punished and those who deserve help should obtain it.

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
Mr. Speaker, before concluding, I hope that some Tory members are compassionate and not merely interested in financial matters. I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is only interested in financial matters, that the dollar and not the human being is essential for him. 1 call on the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) who is the member for Roberval and was a school principal. Perhaps as a school principal he had to be tough. He belongs to a generation where the strap was still in use. Nowadays, things have changed. We now communicate and exchange. The most brilliant children in school are perhaps the most boisterous ones. They used to be those who worked hardest, but things have changed.
Today, some people will make their mark, will innovate, because they wanted to do so and went ahead. They did not fall in line and stick to the rules. And I think that if we consider history, there were many refugees in Canada who were troublemakers. The past is a warrant for the future. Something happens all of a sudden because the Minister of Employment and Immigration thinks all refugees coming to Canada are bad people. That is false. If the Minister is heartless, insensitive, I dare hope that some of the 210 Conservative Members will prove to be humane. I am sure Conservative Members have one or two refugees in their ridings; we all have some. Before voting against the amendments and passing the Bill, they should sit down with those refugees and ask them: "Now, tell me how it was. What did you go through in your country and why did you not stay there? Why did you choose to come in as refugees and not follow the normal immigration procedures?"
After hearing the story of those people, perhaps Conservative Members will see things differently and ask the Minister to change his position and accept my colleague's amendments. Mr. Speaker, I hope this will happen in the next few days.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to what my colleague the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) had to say. He gave a very capable and emotional speech on the refugee Bill. They even went so far as to predict that certain clauses of Bill C-84 would be struck

Perhaps the Hon. Member for Montreal-Saint-Marie (Mr. Malepart) could share his thoughts not on the here and now, but what this law will do, if it is struck down by the courts, to the confidence of Canadians in the system. Member not believe that there is also an international component that Canada, rather than being the leader in this field, will now be a follower and an instigator for other countries to pass the same law? Member not agree by pushing this Bill through that he will be undermining the international strength and resolve needed to try to have an international solution to what is essentially an international problem?

I think that the Winter Games and the sharing of the flame all over Canada by people of all origins and all provinces are proof of our pride and our sense of belonging. And that represents an asset the world over where other countries, perhaps owing to their history, are inclined to act more harshly with one another. Perhaps such a behaviour, such an attitude on the part of Canada might encourage certain individuals who are like our Minister of Employment and Immigration, a man who is wont to take a hard position with respect to these people. We will end up by pushing them back, we will force human beings throughout the world to suffer in their own

country instead of letting some of them come here, not to mention others who have managed to make changes.
I should think that the two questions asked by my colleague. . . but 1 have hope and I have confidence in Quebecers and in Canadians. At the next election they will know what to do with these people. Mr. Speaker, I very much regret that I have to speak on this Bill today because it is the first Bill that was brought before the House of Commons since my election on July 20, 1987.
This Bill was brought before the House as a result of the calling together of the House in an emergency session last summer. Unfortunately for me it was my first experience with the parliamentary process. 1 found it to be a most cynical approach and attitude by the Government toward a situation which occurred involving people coming ashore in the Province of Nova Scotia. The Government thought that it had on its plate an issue through which it could fan some flames in favour of itself and its own purported attempt to take action on what the Government said was a very serious problem.
We were called back and presented with this legislation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spent a fair amount of time during that period trying to convince the people of Canada that this was a most serious problem and in his greatest attempt at sincerity he talked about how his Government would take action in this national emergency. It is now almost six months later and we are still debating this so-called emergency legislation.
It is of great sadness to me as a Canadian to have a Government with the kind of majority which this one has abusing that majority in the face of widespread, virtually unanimous, disagreement and opposition to the kinds of measures that it has taken under this legislation.
Within a matter of days after the legislation had been tabled in the House groups and individuals in Canada who understand international affairs and understand the situation in which people from other countries flee to Canada spoke out against it. There are also groups which support international
Immigration Act, 1976
citizens in their efforts to seek refuge from countries, regimes and governments which do not respect human rights.
Soon after the introduction of this legislation we saw a remarkable thing in this House and I was proud to be a part of it in this respect. I saw principled men and women in this House, men like the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) who took it upon himself the challenge of fighting against the Government, of meeting with groups and individuals who were interested and concerned with what the Government was doing. He spoke out fearlessly on this issue and has tried, unfortunately, without success to convince the Government that it had done the wrong thing. We have seen since then a Government determined in its cynicism to bluff its way to the bitter end on this debate.
We have seen committees of this House and the other place listen to witnesses for many long days on this issue. If there was some sort of national debate about it, if it was a matter of controversy on which men and women of conscience disagreed, we would have had a very different debate and a very different set of hearings than we had.
What did we have? Almost unanimous opposition to the measures taken by the Government and its willingness to ignore the human rights of international citizens. I say almost unanimous because there were some people who spoke at these hearings in support of the legislation. They were the very senior civil servants in the Department of Employment and Immigration. They were doing what their political masters on the other side of the House told them to do. Not one citizen of this country came forward in support of this legislation. Not one, except those who were forced to do so because of the political opportunism of the Government last summer.
As a Canadian I am ashamed to see that the Government has chosen to ignore those citizens and organizations of this country who seek to hold out their hand to these international citizens seeking refuge. My riding does not have very many immigrants, certainly not very many refugees, but I have not had one phone call or letter urging me to support the Government's position on Bill C-84. I have not had a group or individual visiting me on Parliament Hill to suggest that I should support this legislation. Even though there are not pressure groups composed of immigrants or former refugees who are urging me to oppose it, we do have in my riding citizens and organizations who are concerned about what the Government is doing and have urged me to speak out against the legislation and in support of the Senate amendments.
These groups consist of the Roman Catholic Office of Social Action, the Newfoundland and Labrador Human Rights Association, the St. John's Oxfam Committee, the Latin American Support Group, the Institute of Social and Economic Research, Amnesty International Group Sixty and others. You will find those groups repeated in every city across this country, not to mention the towns and villages where such

February 2, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
groups exist who are concerned about human rights and about Canada's reputation in the world for recognition of the international human rights of refugees.
1 have also received from the Primate of the Anglican Church of Canada a representation on the measures proposed by the Senate to amend Bill C-84. That church has a history of involving itself in refugee and other international issues. The concerns expressed by the national Executive Council of the Anglican Church of Canada are that the Bill does not satisfy the international obligations of Canada to protect refugees and uphold procedural safeguards. They are concerned that this legislation violates sections of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. They are concerned that it does not meet the stated objectives of our immigration policy, which is to fulfil Canada's international legal obligations with respect to refugees and uphold its humanitarian traditions with respect to the displaced and persecuted.
Why is it that the United Church of Canada and the other organizations I mentioned have spoken out with one voice against the Government's action, but the Government has not listened? It persists in putting to this House legislation unacceptable to the people of Canada who have studied and understand the issue, who have a concern for Canada's role in international affairs and its obligations to those seeking refuge. The Government persists in its desire to have the power to turn ships around at sea. The Government persists in denying those who claim refugee status the opportunity of a hearing if it has decided that they may be or are accused of being a security risk.
Many people can be abused in very strange circumstances involving international intrigue. Governments of other countries can very easily put forward evidence for the purpose of attempting to get another Government to deny someone entrance or even a hearing to determine whether or not the status of refugee ought to be considered. The Government has insisted on maintaining its stance that criminal prosecutions be maintained for those who encourage or assist people who are attempting entry into this country without the right kind of papers.
The Government's response to the Senate amendments is totally unacceptable. It fails to take into account the concerns raised by the witnesses before the hearings and in this place on many occasions, and is sending us down a road which can only lead to the deterioration of our regard for human rights.
I will end where I started by saying that it is a very sad occasion for me to have to speak on this legislation. It is the first Bill I encountered in this Parliament, brought in in a very cynical way, and it will go out in the same way. The Government will persist in the face of reasoned, impassioned and caring opposition and concern for the human rights of Canadians and those seeking refuge from other countries.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, am disappointed to have to participate in this debate in this way. By "this way" of course I mean that this is the last speech I will be able to make on this legislation. The Government has decided once again to use the strength of its majority to curtail the voice of parliamentarians on this issue. It has used its strength to muzzle Parliament on this issue.
I believe that that is unfortunate for us all because this legislation with regard to immigration and refugees is fundamentally flawed, fundamentally unfair, and fundamentally unjust. I believe that this issue should be taken to the people of Canada in the form of a referendum or plebiscite to learn how they feel about this legislation. I suspect that the reaction in my constituency is similar to that in every constituency across the country. It is overwhelmingly against this legislation.
One might legitimately ask why I say that, what evidence I have to make those comments. I read the transcripts and
Immigration Act, 1976
studied the reports of witnesses who appeared before both the House of Commons committee and the Senate regarding this Bill on immigrants and refugees. I noted an interesting theme. All of those individuals or organizations with considerable experience and expertise on immigration and refugee matters advised the Government not to proceed with the Bill in its present form. The only exception was the witnesses who came on behalf of the Government.
Dozens of individuals and groups, representing hundreds of thousands of Canadians, spoke against this legislation but the Government chose to ignore their suggestions and pleas.
Some of these groups include the Bar Association of Canada, which represents the entire legal profession, the InterChurch Committee on Refugees, which is made up of some nine major denominations of Canada's largest churches, the Canadian Congress of Catholic Bishops, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, the Civil Liberties Association of Canada, the famous Rabbi Gunther Plaut, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the B'Nai Brith group, the Coalition for a Just Refugee and Immigration Policy. They included the Primate of the Anglican Church of Canada.
It is also interesting to point out that among these groups was the employment and immigration union representing those men and women who worked for the immigration office. They spoke against this Bill in many cases, saying that as practitioners in the field who would have to administer this Act, they are against some of its major clauses.
One must ask who favours this legislation. As I look about the country, other than a handful of members of the Conservative Party who are represented by Members in the House, I have not found anyone who supports the legislation. That in itself is condemnation of the Bill, without going into the specifics, as we have.
It is important that we as parliamentarians recognize that the Bill in its present form violates the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in Canada's Constitution. To make matters worse, the Bill violates the United Nations convention on the treatment of refugees. Why would parliamentarians pass legislation that violates our own Constitution and a convention of the United Nations? I have yet to hear why the Government would be encouraged to do that.
I recall a number of occasions when you, Mr. Speaker, spoke of your origins, and, I suspect, reminded me that at the turn of the century when Canada was settled by hundreds of thousands of people from western and central Europe, many of them were fleeing persecution of one kind or another. That is a theme that western Canadians in particular know very well. We know the history of the Mennonites, Hutterites and Doukhobors. We know the more recent history of the Hungarians, Czechoslovakians, Iranians, Afghans, the boat people and Chileans.

What would have happened if the native people of Canada had a similar immigration policy as this after they came to North America via the land bridge tens of thousands of years ago? I suspect that many of us would not be here today.
I vividly recall two events in our recent past. In 1939, Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi persecution in Europe came to Montreal on the ship St. Louis, where the immigration authorities of the day, with the support of the Government of the day, turned the ship back to Europe. Evidence indicates that most of those people on that ship died at the hands of the Nazis. That was a black day in our history which we never want to repeat.
The House will know the story of the Kamagata Maru in 1914. At that time we had a very racist immigration policy which was not entirely above board.
At that time the Government used subtle ways to have a racist immigration policy. The Government of the day did not want East Indians to come to Canada as settlers and therefore had a policy which only allowed people to come to Canada on a steamship that sailed directly from one port to Canada. The Government knew that no steamships came from India.
However, an enterprising individual from Hong Kong obtained a Japanese freighter in 1914, and 376 Punjabs, mostly Sikhs, sailed aboard that ship for Canada and entered the Port of Vancouver. Their entry was essentially legal, which frustrated the immigration authorities. Rather than allow those Sikhs to enter Canada to become citizens, the ship was held in the harbour for two months. The Royal Canadian Navy cruiser Rainbow was brought into the harbour on July 20 and encouraged the Kamagata Maru to sail back to India where many of those people were killed because of rumours about their political and religious beliefs. Again, it was one of the darkest days in our history.
This Bill contains a clause that provides that someone who believes that a ship may contain illegal refugees can order that ship to be turned about. How does one determine whether the people on board such a ship are legal or illegal refugees, whether they are fleeing persecution, or people with no homeland? Yet we are being asked to pass legislation that contains such a vague clause giving that kind of authority to immigration officials.
That is why the men and women of the Employment and Immigration Union came to the committee. They wanted to know whether they will be expected to carry arms on board a ship where someone may have the impression that refugees are on board, to seize the ship, search it and turn it about? They did not receive an acceptable response to those legitimate questions. My colleagues and I want no part of legislation that will do what we did to the Kamagata Maru and the St. Louis. We want no part of legislation that has tinges of racism attached to it. I do not think there is any overt racism, but many people in my constituency have wondered about it.
When I last visited the immigrant centre in my constituency, a number of people wondered if the same concern on the part of the federal Government would have been there if the Tamils who arrived on our East Coast unexpectedly had not been of a visible minority, if they had been people from Poland, from the Soviet Union or from other countries-

The Hon. Member wants to imply that racism is behind the legislation. I hope he would give serious thought to the fact that it has nothing to do with racism. It has everything to do with maintaining the integrity of the system.
As the Hon. Member's colleague from Ottawa Centre said just an hour ago, there are people who have used the refugee system to bypass the immigration system. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre alleged that this was because the immigration system was plugged up. I believe that was the word he used. In effect, he gave credence to the term "jumping the queue".
I hope my friend from Kamloops-Shuswap would think very carefully before he imputes motives of racism to this legislation or to any other legislation this Government puts before the House.
